innovations.name: Warm Rotterdam
innovations.problem:
Rotterdam is the poorest city in the Netherlands. About 18.5 percent of Rotterdammers live below the poverty line. That is more than 87,000 Rotterdammers who can no longer provide for the basic necessities of life. In some districts of the city, a quarter to a third of the inhabitants live in poverty. One in every six children in Rotterdam grows up in a poor family.
Of these people in poverty, more than half have been living on a low income for four years or more. These people have no financial reserves. A financial setback has major consequences. Small debts grow into substantial amounts, partly due to collection costs associated with these debts
innovations.desc:
In 2016, the Pauluskerk (a church) started the Warm Rotterdam program. In 2019, Warm Rotterdam became an independent foundation. We are a network organisation of experts and partners. Our experts are experts by experience. Our partners include companies, the government and civil society organisations. Together we are committed to reducing the number of Rotterdammers in poverty. We raise awareness about poverty and develop effective approaches. To this end, we mobilize and bundle the knowledge and experiences of Rotterdammers who know what it is like to live in poverty and with debts. Additionally, we put system errors on the agenda and we encourage everyone to support our goal of chasing poverty out of the city
Our experts by experience are the basis of Warm Rotterdam. We listen to them because they know how disruptive (long-term) living in poverty and debt is. They also know what would…
innovations.target: Homeless persons, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence:
We come up with concrete solutions, such as sample letters, the basic shopping list ( de basisboodschappenlijst ), the Tobia (Tijdelijke Overbruggingskrediet Burgers in Armoede ), Warm Consultation Hours and the Quality Mark Warm Collection (Keurmerk Warm Incasseren).
We make Rotterdam aware of poverty, for example through our YouTube campaigns ‘ Armoede Voor Beginners’ en ‘Rotterdam slaat terug tegen armoede’ or the '50 euro challenge' in which we challenged politicians to live on 50 euros a week.

innovations.name: RaumBooster
innovations.problem: Many local makers, small businesses, and cultural initiatives face high barriers when trying to access or activate affordable spaces. Activation costs such as deposits, renovation, or equipment often exceed their financial capacity, while public funding requires own contributions they cannot provide. At the same time, many ground-floor spaces remain vacant. This mismatch blocks social, cultural, and economic potential at neighbourhood level.
innovations.desc:
The RaumBooster introduces a cooperative matchfunding model that links community crowdfunding with public and private co-funding. It lowers entry barriers for local initiatives by rewarding civic engagement with additional grants once a defined crowdfunding threshold is reached. This hybrid mechanism mobilises new resources, activates vacant spaces, and creates a replicable model for social innovation and local economic resilience.
The model was piloted in Vienna and Graz, and later adapted in Innsbruck through the “Aufrunden bitte” mechanism. In 2025, the concept evolved into WeCreateSpace, a co-financing system that structurally links crowdfunding with public funding schemes. It is also being applied in sheBOOST to mobilise community resources for women-led local makers.
innovations.target: Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence: The pilots in Vienna, Graz demonstrated strong leverage effects: every euro of matchfunding mobilised up to 22 euros in community contributions. Seven campaigns enabled the activation or renovation of several spaces, including cultural centres and creative hubs. The model proved that combining public, private, and civic funds increases participation, strengthens local networks, and makes urban transformation more inclusive and effective.

innovations.name: Solidary Europe for Inclusive Society
innovations.problem: Vocational education and training (VET) schools in Croatia provide significantly fewer learning opportunities related to the European Union compared to general secondary schools. As a result, many VET students have limited knowledge about EU institutions, values, rights and opportunities for participation. Teachers and school librarians often lack the competences, tailored resources and confidence to integrate EU topics into their teaching practice, which deepens inequality in civic education and student engagement. This gap contributes to lower levels of active citizenship and social inclusion among young people in VET pathways, particularly those coming from disadvantaged regions or…
innovations.desc: EUsolis introduced a new model of EU citizenship education in vocational schools by empowering both teachers and school librarians as co-creators of learning, rather than relying solely on traditional civics instruction. The project developed a structured modular curriculum tailored to the VET context, focusing on solidarity, diversity, youth participation and sustainable development, and demonstrated how these EU values can be meaningfully incorporated into any subject area. By using school libraries and the European Documentation Centre as active learning hubs, the project expanded access to EU knowledge beyond the classroom. Practical workshops, regional Spring and Summer Schools and open digital resources ensured that educators could immediately transfer new knowledge into school activities, creating a sustainable and scalable model for inclusive EU learning across VET systems.
innovations.target: NEETs (Not in Education, Employment, or Training), Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Other target groups
innovations.benef: Faculty of Economics and Business University of Zagreb
innovations.evidence: EUsolis successfully improved access to EU-related learning in vocational education by building the competences of teachers and school librarians across Croatia. More than 50 educators from 15 VET schools participated in specialised training and regional capacity-building events, enabling them to integrate EU values into everyday teaching and school library activities. Four thematic educational modules and a complete set of open-access learning materials were developed to support continued use after the project’s end. The project strengthened collaboration among VET schools, created new…
authors: Faculty of Economics and Business University of Zagreb

innovations.name: JOIN-UA-EMPLOY
innovations.problem: Across the EU, displaced Ukrainians face fragmented services, language barriers, and slow recognition of skills, resulting in under-employment and prolonged welfare dependence.
innovations.desc: The project introduces a portable skills profile, common referral and case-management standards, and a shared employer-engagement playbook. It integrates quick language-on-the-job modules with sector-specific matching and uses real-time feedback loops (dashboards and learning reviews) so PES teams can adjust support rapidly and consistently across countries.
innovations.target: Migrants and ethnic minorities, Long-term or repeatedly unemployed persons, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence: Pilots are expected to shorten time-to-first job, increase the share of quality placements (stable contracts, fair wages), and raise employer satisfaction. Beneficiaries gain faster access to suitable work and progression routes; PES gain reusable tools, staff training packages, and comparative evidence on “what works,” reducing cost per successful placement.

This multi-dimensional methodology addresses the interconnected barriers refugees face, ranging from skills gaps and cultural adaptation to discrimination and family responsibilities, in a single, coordinated framework.

innovations.problem:
Households increasingly face challenges in the liberalized energy market : rising prices, lack of transparency, and difficulty accessing renewable sources. At the same time, social inequalities persist—especially for people with disabilities who struggle to find affordable and inclusive housing. Traditional welfare systems and isolated sustainability initiatives have proved insufficient to connect environmental goals with tangible social inclusion . The key problem is how to combine the energy transition with community welfare in a fair, participatory, and economically viable way.

innovations.name: Villages Vivants
innovations.problem: In many rural areas, empty shops and closed shutters are a common sight. When a café, bakery, or grocery store closes, daily services and community life disappear with it. Yet local initiatives are flourishing. An abandoned factory can become a shared space for 50 people. A bookstore, a bike repair workshop, or a reuse center can breathe new life into rural areas. Every day, these communities are reinventing local consumption and solidarity. They respond to real local needs and focus on social impact, not profit. They are close to people, fostering connection and community. However, these initiatives often face significant challenges to settle in rural areas, such as accessing high-quality,…
innovations.desc:
Villages Vivants is a rural, citizen-driven, and solidarity-focused cooperative that buys, renovates, and rents premises to host activities with social impact in rural areas. We support social and solidarity economy projects, unconventional initiatives, citizen-led dynamics, and shared spaces, helping to revitalize villages and foster community life. We also partner with local authorities and collectives with real estate projects. Through solidarity-based investments from citizens and partners, Villages Vivants can acquire new premises, strengthen its social impact, and contribute to vibrant, thriving rural communities.
This project has been developed in close collaboration with numerous local development actors and rural stakeholders, such as Terre de Liens, Habitat et Humanisme, GRAP, Ronalpia, URSCOP, Grenade...

Residents can participate as volunteers, customers, donors, investors, employees, or decision-makers in their village’s projects. By facilitating access to the premises, we make it easier for these initiatives to get off the ground and help ensure their long-term sustainability.

innovations.name: YoU Decide - Supporting Displaced Youth of Ukraine in Making Informed Decisions
innovations.problem: The project addresses the risks faced by displaced Ukrainian youth during their transition into adulthood, including limited access to reliable information, fragmented support systems, and heightened vulnerability to exploitation and exclusion. By understanding their specific needs and tailoring solutions through safe digital tools, dialogue with local stakeholders, and awareness raising, the project seeks to close critical gaps in integration and ensure that young people can access the rights and opportunities essential for their well-being and future.
innovations.desc: The You Decide project introduces a digital “one-stop shop” app that provides displaced youth with safe, localised, and multilingual access to services and support systems in their place of residence. What makes this approach innovative is its participatory design: Ukrainian youth are directly engaged in co-developing project tools, ensuring that the solutions are relevant, user-friendly, and truly meet the needs of the target group. This combination of technology and youth-led design bridges existing gaps in information access and integration support.

innovations.desc: The project introduces an innovative universal design of educational materials, integrating neuropsychology and emotional self-regulation insights. The solution includes methodological material, reflection and situation cards, posters for self-reflection and self-regulation skills, a guide, and lesson plans. These resources are visually appealing, playful, and practical, ensuring inclusivity and emotional development in schools, day care centers, and homes.

Faculty staff spends approximately 24 thousand hours annually to manually check theses formatting and citations. During peak submission periods, this workload becomes unmanageable. High resubmission rates lead to graduation delays, as each rejected thesis requires another round of manual review, creating a cascade of inefficiency. Manual checking is also inconsistent, as some errors are caught while others slip through, leaving students with a perception of arbitrariness in the process, and the faculty with the perception of rules inconsistencies. Additionally, students struggle with…
innovations.desc: TechCheck & Cite offer a joint solution that redefines how academic writing and digital literacy are supported. While many tools focus on literature reviews (fostering academic indecency), mere reference management or plagiarism detection, none address the technical dimensions of academic writing: technical editing, formatting, structure, presentation and citations all at once. TechCheck combines educational guidance with automated technical checks, ensuring documents consistently meet institutional standards. Within this ecosystem, Cite functions both as a dedicated module as well as a standalone solution powered by a custom-built citation algorithm based on over 100 hours of researching academic writing rules of all Slovenian faculties and major internationally used citation and referencing styles. This foundation enables automated, accurate verification of citations and references —…

For students and researchers, it provides interactive, real-time feedback, building both digital literacy and academic writing skills. By detecting and correcting errors early, TechCheck reduces the number of resubmissions, helping prevent delays in graduation or publication. innovations.name: SciComic
innovations.problem: On one hand, one in seven people have some kind of learning difficulties such as dyslexia, ADHD or dyspraxia. These challenges do not reflect intelligence, but rather the need for alternative learning methods. Because of this, two-thirds of such students never obtain a university degree, as highly specialised language makes traditional academic texts often inaccessible. Current adaptations in educational systems are limited and mostly targeted at primary and secondary schools, leaving university students without sufficient support. Students often resort to time-consuming methods such as animated educational videos or expensive private tutoring, which are unsustainable solutions in the long…
innovations.desc: SciComic is the world’s first complex-to-simple translator that utilises innovative technology to transform complex research papers into popular-science comics. By integrating multiple leading large language models with prompt engineering, keyword mapping, tailored illustrations and our own state-of-the-art fact verification loop, our web app enables students with learning difficulties to comprehend research papers quickly and effectively, while also helping researchers reach a wider audience. Unlike existing adaptations that mainly focus on intermediary switches between reading and listening, as well as unreliable generative AI tools, SciComic provides inclusive support for a broader spectrum of learning difficulties, reducing cognitive load and offering alternative learning formats. Built with scalable technologies such as Node.js, React and TypeScript, and supported by PostgreSQL and…

innovations.problem: Displaced individuals from Ukraine face multiple challenges as they seek stability and integration in the Baltic states. Many struggle to find employment that matches their qualifications or lack the skills required by the local labor market, creating significant employment and skills gaps. Language barriers and limited knowledge of local culture, systems, and norms further hinder integration efforts. These challenges often contribute to social exclusion, loneliness, and psychological distress, leaving many displaced persons feeling isolated from their new communities. innovations.desc: The ESSI-BALTIC project introduces a combination of creative, cross-sector approaches to support displaced Ukrainians and strengthen regional collaboration. One key innovation is the development of digital information platforms, such as apps or websites, designed to centralize essential resources, provide real-time updates, and create an accessible Q&A hub for displaced persons. The project also implements community-driven integration models, including buddy programs, cultural clubs, and grassroots events, to foster meaningful connections between displaced individuals and host communities. These initiatives promote inclusion through personal interaction and mutual learning, rather than relying solely on institutional support. Another innovation is the cross-border cooperation framework. By uniting the Red Cross Societies of Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia, the project ensures the…

innovations.evidence: The ESSI-BALTIC project will deliver measurable improvements in the lives of displaced Ukrainians while strengthening regional collaboration across the Baltic states. Through personalized job counselling, vocational training, and entrepreneurship initiatives, participants will gain the skills and confidence needed to secure meaningful employment. Focused language programs and cultural orientation activities will enhance communication and understanding, enabling smoother integration into host communities. innovations.name: „Culture360.ai – AI platform for CCI funding applications and business plans“
innovations.problem: Across the CCI sector, especially outside big cities, preparing grant applications and strategic documents is slow, costly and uncertain. Information on funding is fragmented across portals; formal PFSA/LKT/EU templates are complex; budget/KPI logic varies; and organisations lack in-house skills to meet compliance, language and formatting standards. Paying consultants is expensive and excludes smaller players. Generic AI assistants are not trained on Lithuanian/CCI specifics, don’t integrate cultural/funding datasets and produce outputs that require heavy manual fixing. These barriers reduce submission quality and volume, delay projects, and deepen inequalities between well-resourced…
innovations.desc: Culture360.ai introduces a sector-specific, compliance-first approach to document creation in CCI. The platform orchestrates LT/EN language models with a rules engine that encodes PFSA/LKT/EU templates (sections, length, required annexes) and a budget/KPI builder with pre-tested formulas. Live connectors aggregate funding calls and cultural market data; users get context-aware suggestions (eligibility, evaluation criteria, indicators) inside the editor. A validator flags gaps (e.g., missing outputs, weak risk logic), while versioned exports produce submission-ready Word/PDF packages. Unlike generic AI, Culture360.ai is trained on CCI terminology and Lithuanian specifics, integrates public datasets, and enforces structure and metrics end-to end. This reduces errors and rework, standardises quality across small/regional organisations, and enables faster, fairer access to funding. The…

innovations.name: SoliCycle
innovations.problem: Every year large numbers of bicycles become waste while many urban residents lack affordable, reliable transport and access to job-training opportunities. Local authorities and waste centres need scalable solutions to divert bike waste from disposal, and socially vulnerable people need practical routes to employment. SoliCycle addresses both environmental (waste, loss of reusable material) and social (unemployment, skills gap, mobility access) problems.
innovations.desc: SoliCycle’s innovation is an integrated, localised “repair-and-insertion” workshop model that: (1) sources large volumes of discarded bikes from déchetteries and community collections; (2) combines professional refurbishment and parts recovery with low-cost sales (often €50–€150) and community self-repair workshops; and (3) embeds a social insertion pathway by hiring trainees on supported contracts to carry out the technical refurbishment and gain job skills — creating a circular, social enterprise loop. SoliCycle was the first project of this sort in 2007, when the first workshop was opened.
innovations.target: Migrants and ethnic minorities, Long-term or repeatedly unemployed persons, NEETs (Not in Education, Employment, or Training)
innovations.evidence:
Proven diversion and reuse: in 2024 SoliCycle recovered 2,500 bicycles and sold 1,258 refurbished bikes along with 2,862 second-hand parts—preventing large volumes of bike waste and extending product lifecycles. Social impact : the workshops operate as insertion projects (e.g., ~12 people on insertion contracts in one site), providing practical training and employment pathways. Immediate social & skills impact (current staff survey):
97% of surveyed employees feel useful in their work.
100% say they do useful work.
62% say they learned to work in a team.

innovations.name: Transformative Tourism in Practice
innovations.problem: The employment rate of people with disabilities in Hungary remains significantly below the EU average. In many cases, monotonous work takes place in segregated conditions. Hungarian society does not consider people with disabilities to be employable. Negative stereotypes and limited direct interaction contribute to their exclusion from the labour market and society. There was a need for a service model that enables inclusion through real-life, shared experiences.
innovations.desc: To achieve a long-term and profound change in attitude at both the individual and community levels, positive experiences are needed for everyone involved that can override previous negative biases. To this end, the project introduced a new model of transformative tourism, where people with disabilities play an active, public-facing role in their work. The initiative combines employment creation with awareness-raising through interactive tourism packages. In addition to employing people with disabilities, it creates an interactive environment that provides all stakeholders with the opportunity for experience-based learning. Visitors pay for the programs, making the service sustainable and scalable.
innovations.target: Individuals with disabilities
innovations.evidence: 5 inclusive tourism packages developed Over 6,000 visitor days in 2023–2024 10 schools and 250 students involved in the pilot Active partnerships with companies and municipalities Paid employment created for people with disabilities Model included in tourism promotion platforms (e.g., pontMiskolc)

innovations.name: Local Innovation Management Model (LIMM)
innovations.problem: Ageing populations are transforming social and economic structures, requiring municipalities to move from administrative to managerial and strategic roles. However, neither local administrations nor communities are adequately prepared for this shift. Traditional approaches fail to foster inclusive innovation or systemic responses. There is an increasing need for innovative thinking and planning renewal, in which stakeholders are also involved. Both the local government apparatus and the local social environment must be prepared for this.
innovations.desc: LIMM introduced a participatory, innovation-driven model for local ageing strategies. It combined societal diagnosis, stakeholder engagement, and planning tools to create the foundation for a local Innovation Point. In the process, they examined public thinking related to aging, support for innovative thinking in the local government and local society, the antecedents that help change attitudes and incorporate innovative methods, and the brakes on the system. The approach supports municipalities in becoming innovation enablers and strategic actors in ageing-related issues.
innovations.target: Other target groups
innovations.evidence:
Achieving openness and understanding in the paradigm-shifting treatment of the aging problem
Participatory workshops held with decision-makers, employers, and civil society
Local attitudes and barriers to innovation mapped
Project Founding Document (PAD) developed with clear goals, indicators, planned activities, and sustainability paths
Joint planning experience gained with the municipality
Methods collected for stakeholder involvement and local adaptation

innovations.name: CEGLAB – The Cegléd Volunteering Platform
innovations.problem: Despite its benefits, volunteering often lacks motivation or incentives for sustained participation. In many communities, a lack of engagement threatens the continuity of civil initiatives. Young people in particular are not easily mobilised without tangible rewards or digital solutions that match their lifestyle.
innovations.desc: CEGLAB introduced a blockchain-powered digital reward system where volunteering is tracked and rewarded with CEGLAB points. These can be redeemed at participating local businesses. A circular model allows businesses to return unused points to civil or public organisations for redistribution, maintaining community flow. The system creates an ecosystem of value exchange, making volunteering more visible, traceable, and appealing.

innovations.evidence: Two competency tests developed and validated (for employees and leaders) Structured feedback and development recommendations provided Use cases confirmed for hiring, talent management, and job satisfaction improvement SME leaders supported in developing conscious leadership skills Conceptualised a future AI-supported “competency marketplace"

innovations.name: Stress Relief and Mental Vitality – A Therapeutic Yoga-Based Training for Holistic Well-being
innovations.problem: Growing mental overload, emotional stress, and value disorientation in society have led to rising rates of anxiety, depression, and burnout. Traditional solutions often lack integration of body-mind approaches. There is a need for holistic, evidence-based practices that enhance resilience and promote sustainable well-being.
innovations.desc: The training combines yoga therapy, cognitive restructuring, and traditional wellness systems (Ayurveda, meditation) in a structured and repeatable programme. It is grounded in scientific validation using nine standardised psychological scales measuring 23 indicators. Participants showed significant improvements in areas like insomnia, self-worth, hopelessness, anxiety, and social functioning.
innovations.target: Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised
innovations.evidence: Training delivered through 6–10 structured group sessions Home-based practice model developed 90% of participants reported significant improvement in multiple mental health domains Normalisation of clinical-level values in anxiety, depression, and sleep disorders Published evaluation using nine validated psychological assessments

innovations.name: Establishing a Local Development Cooperation Forum Model
innovations.problem: Lack of cooperation among local organisations often leads to fragmented services, inefficiencies, and limited access for residents. Even organisations under the same ownership or sector frequently do not engage in joint planning. Larger towns face particular challenges due to the number of actors and lack of coordination mechanisms.
innovations.desc: The project introduced a local forum model to create structured dialogue and collaborative planning among similar-service organisations. It engaged stakeholders in mapping cooperation potential and developing a joint vision. The method helped identify short- and long-term development opportunities and inspired follow-up initiatives such as a sports guide and public fair.
innovations.target: Other target groups
innovations.evidence: 3-part local forum held with NGOs, sport clubs, and city representatives Increased collaboration between sports organisations Launch of the SPORTKALAUZ Szombathely online guide Development and implementation of the Sport Fair (Sportbörze) concept Strengthened relationships and joint planning culture across the sector

innovations.name: Easing the Kindergarten-to-School Transition Through Sport and Music
innovations.problem: Many children entering school show large developmental gaps—up to two years—particularly in segregated areas. They lack access to cultural and physical activities that support learning, such as music and sports, which deepens educational inequalities and limits future opportunities.
innovations.desc: The project integrated body-based and experiential learning using music and wrestling as development tools. Through games, rhythm, and movement, children developed fundamental skills without formal instruction. The method supported cognitive, social, and emotional development while building bridges between families, teachers, and local institutions.
innovations.target: Other target groups
innovations.evidence: Children showed improved language and reading skills Better spatial and temporal orientation Greater self-confidence and classroom engagement Parents became more involved in the educational process The first cohort’s wrestling team placed 4th at a national school competition

innovations.name: Felirom.hu – Smart Notebook and Web Application for Small-scale Farmers
innovations.problem: Small producers face major challenges in managing mandatory records related to production, processing, packaging, and sales. Traditional tools are inefficient and error-prone, making compliance and business optimisation difficult.
innovations.desc:
Felirom.hu is a cloud-based web application designed by and for small-scale producers. It simplifies daily tasks through modular data entry, improves transparency and traceability, and enables better production planning. Continuous user testing ensured the system aligns with real needs.
The innovation of Felirom.hu goes significantly beyond technological solutions available on the commercial market. Its uniqueness primarily lies in the participatory action research methodology employed in its creation. Unlike standard commercial apps—which are typically designed for larger-scale agricultural producers, require high-level digital literacy, and involve considerable expenses—our application was co-designed directly with small-scale producers through intensive, bottom-up engagement processes within an EIP-AGRI operational group.
This participatory approach allowed us to specifically tailor…
innovations.target: Other target groups
innovations.evidence: Easy-to-use admin platform for small producers Improved regulatory compliance and risk reduction Better forecasting of production peaks Enhanced planning of supplies and packaging Built-in adaptability for future features and integration

innovations.name: Conflict Management in Healthcare – Training Programme for Health Professionals
innovations.problem: Good communication is one of the most critical factors in healing work. Healthcare settings often generate conflict both among professionals and between staff and patients due to complexity, stress, and vulnerability. This is partly because healthcare is a highly complex environment at both professional and organizational levels. At the same time, patients are already in a more vulnerable state because of the worry and stress related to their health. Miscommunication and unresolved disputes reduce team effectiveness, compromise well-being, and increase the risk of patient harm.
innovations.desc:
In response to this situation, we have developed a training program for healthcare professionals in collaboration with the Foundation for Women in Healthcare (Gyógyító Nőkért Alapítvány). The program supports and strengthens the conflict-management strategies of doctors, nurses, psychologists, and other healthcare professionals in their interprofessional relationships and interactions with patients and their relatives. Effective conflict management is crucial because it contributes to improved collaboration among colleagues, the preservation of their mental well-being, and safer patient care.
The program is available as an accredited, credit-awarding OFTEX course for physicians (Continuing Medical Education), including both theoretical and practical modules. The first training session was held on April 4, 2025, and included 34 healthcare workers. Our training is also open to healthcare…
innovations.target: Other target groups
innovations.evidence:
-Greater teamwork among medical professionals -Improved emotional resilience in high-stress environments -Safer and more responsive patient care -Integration of research from over 300 international healthcare cases -Adaptability for a range of medical settings and professions
Feedback from the first training:
’What I really liked was that the training exercises were based on real situations.’
‘I particularly liked the interactive exercises, especially when we had to visualize a conflict situation on a sheet of paper.’
’I liked that we listened to lectures first and then did the group…

innovations.name: Asertos Programme
innovations.problem: The Valencia Region has gone from having 12.3% of its population living in vulnerable neighbourhoods in 1991 to 43% in 2011, the highest rate in mainland Spain. The regional observatory data shows that in 2020 the most affected province was Alicante, with 26.31% of its population residing in areas of low vulnerability, 33.09% in areas of medium vulnerability and 12.19% in areas of integral vulnerability; in total, almost three quarters of the provincial population. Urban Vulnerability is a Public Health problem encouraged by urban segregation, a process of exclusion that confines populations with disadvantaged situations in specific territories. It is a direct result of the real estate…
innovations.desc: The greatest difference between Asertos and other urban regeneration or community development programmes, is that we assert that the analysis of the problems and their impact on people only offers us a partial reality. In order to understand these ecosystems from their complexity, it is essential to complement the needs-centred view (deficit or pathogenic approach) with a view that focuses on strengths (salutogenic approach). The Salutogenic Theory offers us a theoretical framework from the paradigm of health creation, which we can operationalize by means of the asset model. On the other hand, we consider the Diffusion of innovations Theory as the framework in which to project social change. Change moves at the speed of trust. That is why if we aspire to change people's behaviours, we have to foster trusting relationships. In order to bring about social change, an active search for…
innovations.target: Migrants and ethnic minorities, Long-term or repeatedly unemployed persons, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence:
This innovation was initially implemented in a single neighbourhood but has since been replicated in five different areas within the same city, adapting the approach to diverse socio-spatial contexts. The methodology has attracted interest from other territories, leading to ongoing collaborations to adapt the solution in Valencia and Almería. Additionally, through a current Erasmus+ project, we are exploring pathways to scale and transfer the model at the European level, while learning from the experiences of partner organisations in France and Ireland.
During the 7 years of work in the…

innovations.name: onCOGITE Workshops to Reconnect the Brain After Cancer
innovations.problem: onCOGITE offers a programme of about twenty cognitive rehabilitation sessions that continues to welcome an increasing number of beneficiaries, with over 90% satisfaction. Our platform allows beneficiaries to book appointments more than two months in advance and enables smooth organisation of videoconferences with their neuropsychologist. A web application supports and intensifies the final phase of the rehabilitation journey by enabling autonomous practice for one year.
innovations.target: Individuals with disabilities, Other target groups
innovations.evidence:
The organisation of workshops, offering a wide range of about 100 online sessions from Monday morning to Saturday noon, allows our beneficiaries to follow the programme consistently with maximum comfort and flexibility at a reduced cost.
This regularity of weekly sessions ensures good cognitive recovery from 15 sessions onwards, as demonstrated by the randomized "e-oncogite" study led by the Labpsy at Bordeaux University, to be published in autumn 2025 (see attached files).
This programme is particularly suited for individuals wishing to return to work after a 1 to 2-year medical leave for…

innovations.name: Participatory Local Governance
innovations.problem: In Hungarian municipalities, especially in rural areas, there is little space for structured public dialogue. As a result, valuable local knowledge, creativity, and relationships remain untapped in planning and development.
innovations.desc: While based on well-known participatory methods, the project’s innovation lies in how these tools were combined and applied in an integrated, community-friendly way. This created a replicable model for participatory governance even in low-capacity settings.
innovations.target: Other target groups
innovations.evidence: Launch of the Bérbaltavár Dialogues, a monthly civic discussion forum Locally defined development actions that require minimal external funding Reconnection of citizens with local heritage and identity Stronger trust and collaboration between residents and the local council Creation of a practical guide and training plan for municipal actors

innovations.name: TAPASZ – Teachers’ Alliance for Solidarity
innovations.problem: Families increasingly seek learning support outside the formal education system, yet lack access to trustworthy, affordable alternatives. Decisions are often based on price or hearsay, without guidance on what best supports the child’s development. Private tutoring remains fragmented, limiting quality and access.
innovations.desc: TAPASZ supported tutors in becoming social entrepreneurs: offering fair-priced, inclusive services while building strong ties to local communities. The initiative introduced new learning formats—teacher lounges, parent-student meetups—within a growing teacher-developer network. Solidarity and sustainability were embedded in everyday practice.

innovations.name: From Idea to Action: Establishing and Operating Social Farms in Practice
innovations.problem: Marginalised groups often lack meaningful employment and social inclusion opportunities. While social farming offers proven benefits, knowledge and support structures for launching such initiatives remain scarce in Hungary. The lack of a regulatory framework and tailored methodology hinders growth.
innovations.desc: The project compiled a step-by-step methodology to establish and sustain social farms. It was validated through direct work with existing farms and pilot mentoring of new ones. Dissemination included professional training and targeted policy proposals. Innovation lies in its cross-sectoral approach, including agricultural, legal, and social expertise.
innovations.target: Individuals with disabilities
innovations.evidence: Practical handbook for social farm creation (ISBN registered, shared with ministries and national institutions) 10 new social farm initiatives launched with mentoring support 15 pilot applicants, of which 10 proved viable National training and regional dissemination events (Budapest, Komárom, Miskolc) Ongoing pro bono support to pilot farms through 2024 Strengthened national network (40+ organisations) Contribution to inclusive rural employment and sustainable local development

innovations.name: Taboo-Free Zone – Sex Education Drama Workshops for Teachers
innovations.problem: Sexuality is a constant presence in students' lives, but teacher training lacks adequate tools to address it. Educators often face situations they cannot ignore, yet feel unprepared to respond appropriately. This gap increases vulnerability and limits effective dialogue in schools.
innovations.desc: The project combined sex education with drama-based learning, creating a safe space where teachers could explore sensitive topics through roleplay, shared reflection, and interactive methods. It not only transferred knowledge but also supported mindset shifts and long-term attitudinal change.
innovations.target: Other target groups
innovations.evidence: Teachers gained tools and confidence to integrate sexuality education into their classrooms Taboos were openly addressed through guided conversations and activities A detailed session plan was created for future use by other educators Drama pedagogy proved effective for processing personal and social issues Students can now better understand their bodies, recognize abuse, and access child protection mechanisms

innovations.name: MEETT (Migration Education Evaluation Transformative Tools)
innovations.problem: Migration policies and public discourses across Europe have become increasingly restrictive, contributing to fear, misinformation, and social polarization. Despite the vital contributions of migrants, their stories are often reduced to numbers or threats, limiting empathy and social cohesion. There is a lack of shared tools and frameworks to evaluate and demonstrate the transformative impact of migration education in this context. MEETT addresses this gap by supporting practitioners with accessible M&E tools to promote inclusive narratives and evidence-based advocacy.
innovations.desc: MEETT develops a shared framework and interactive M&E tools specifically tailored to migration education. By co-creating these tools with field practitioners across Europe, the project ensures their relevance, adaptability, and usability. This approach empowers youth workers and educators to measure and showcase the social impact of their work, reinforcing advocacy efforts with concrete data. MEETT also fosters cross-border collaboration, contributing to the professionalization and recognition of migration education as a lever for social transformation.
innovations.target: Migrants and ethnic minorities, Other target groups
innovations.evidence: - A shared European framework for monitoring and evaluating migration education initiatives; - A toolkit of adaptable, interactive M&E tools co-designed with youth workers and educators; - Strengthened capacities of field actors to assess and communicate the impact of their work; - Increased visibility and legitimacy of migration education among policymakers and the media; - Enhanced cross-border collaboration and knowledge-sharing within the sector; - A contribution to more inclusive, cohesive societies through evidence-based advocacy and educational practices.

innovations.name: Social aspects of digital intelligence
innovations.problem: Digital intelligence is essential for modern society and the economy. It involves not only technological skills, but also critical thinking and responsible use of technology. Measuring and developing digital intelligence at both the societal and enterprise level is essential for successful digitalisation. As the digital society evolves, inequalities in digital literacy and infrastructure development are also emerging. In rural areas, lack of infrastructure and limited skills can be barriers to accessing online education and other digital services. Research on the social impact of digitalisation emphasises that the success of social innovation depends on the empowerment and involvement of…
innovations.desc: The biggest achievement of the research team was the creation of the Digital Intelligence Profile (DIP) digital intelligence scale, following the steps of the scale validation process and registering the trademark in Hungarian and English. The Digital Intelligence Profile (DIP) measures 8 dimensions (Digital Personality, Digital Harmony, Digital Risk, Digital Protection, Digital Emotional Intelligence, Digital Dialogue, Digital Literacy, Digital Empowerment), 3 levels (basic, advanced, expert), 3 domains (knowledge, skills, attitudes).
innovations.target: Other target groups

It is therefore important to measure and improve it so that everyone has access to digital technologies. - Education and participation. - Resilience: digital intelligence is a foundation for resilience, especially in crisis situations such as the Covid-19 pandemic. innovations.name: LEARNING BY DOING
innovations.problem: The starting point was alarming: 63% of Roma youth were neither studying nor working, and 86% were living in poverty conditions. Access to employment became an urgent matter.
innovations.desc: The project’s innovative nature lies in: -An experiential learning methodology, with six-month theoretical-practical pathways in real companies. -A strategic alliance with more than 60 companies in key sectors, which not only collaborate but also co-designed and delivered part of the training. -The use of social support as an equity mechanism, preventing family poverty from becoming a barrier to participation. -A rigorous selection system that prioritises potential and competencies over traditional employability criteria. -Integration with professional teams from the Acceder program, specialised in intercultural mediation and individualized social mentoring.
innovations.target: Migrants and ethnic minorities, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence: Between 2013 and 2023, thanks to the efforts of 170 professionals from our organisation, more than 3,500 young people—90% of whom were Roma and nearly 70% without formal education and facing major structural barriers (poverty, segregation, discrimination)—joined this innovative training model. This model focused on competency development in real work settings, with intensive professional support and public-private partnerships in 41 cities.

innovations.name: Rejoué
innovations.problem:
Rejoué addresses several social and environmental challenges:
Toy waste: Millions of toys are discarded each year, often while still usable. Rejoué helps reduce this waste by giving toys a second life through reuse and refurbishment.
Social exclusion: Many people face long-term unemployment and difficulties entering the job market. Rejoué offers integration pathways through paid work, training, and individualized support.
Inequality in access to toys: Not all families can afford quality toys. Rejoué makes toys accessible to all by offering refurbished items at low cost or donating them to those in need.
Overconsumption and environmental impact: By promoting reuse, Rejoué encourages more…
innovations.desc:
Rejoué offers an innovative solution by combining environmental impact, social inclusion, and educational value in a single model:
Circular economy applied to toys: Rejoué pioneers the reuse of toys on a large scale, implementing rigorous processes for sorting, cleaning, and safety-checking items, which is rare in this sector.
Social integration through meaningful work: Rejoué involves people in reintegration programs across all stages of toy refurbishment, providing hands-on experience, personalized support, and skill-building opportunities that foster long-term employability. A key specificity of Rejoué is its strong focus on supporting women, particularly those facing multiple barriers to employment. Few integration workshops in France are tailored to women’s needs—Rejoué fills this gap with a supportive and adapted work environment.
Educational and awareness-raising actions: Rejoué…

Social inclusion: Rejoué supports around 70 people per year through its integration workshop, with a majority of participants being women. Many of them move on to stable employment or vocational training thanks to personalized support and skills development. Access to quality toys: Thousands of refurbished toys are made available each year at affordable prices or through donations, helping families in need…

innovations.name: SPORT IN HOSPITALS
innovations.problem: • Break the boredom imposed by prolonged hospitalization, sometimes far from parents and siblings. Psychological benefits such as smiles and laughter are the most common comments. • Promote care as a comprehensive approach: not just blood tests, treatments, and infusions, but also personal development and the discovery of new sports activities. • Educate children on the basics of healthy sports and thus prove to them that whatever their limitations and disabilities related to the disease, physical activity is possible. Indeed, the immediate physical benefits, such as better breathing control, reassurance regarding physical activity, and an improvement in chronic pain.
innovations.desc: To ensure optimal care, we offer team sports sessions, allowing children to break their isolation and rediscover the joy of "sharing together" through sports. Today, this isolation has increased following the COVID-19 epidemic. With this in mind, Premiers de Cordée aims to offer healthcare facilities a more comprehensive and personalized approach. This offer comes at a material and human cost, but the stakes are high. A sick child is an athlete in their own way. Like a top-level athlete, they fight tenaciously every day to surpass their limits and achieve their goal: recovery.
innovations.target: Individuals with disabilities
innovations.evidence:
Quantitative objectives : * 14,000 Children benefit from our programmes (2024 figures) * 100 Paediatric service everywhere in France (2024 figures) * 1,056 Sports demos and taster sessions (2024 figures) Qualitative objectives : • Develop social connections • Improve the well-being of hospitalized children • Develop self-esteem and self-confidence • Change perceptions of the hospital
It is already scaled up in Hauts-de-France, Nouvelle Aquitaine, Provence Alpes Côte d'Azur, Auvergne Rhône Alpes, Grand Est, Normandie, Pays de la Loire

innovations.name: Living Life Counselling
innovations.problem:
Ireland has long struggled with underfunded and overburdened public mental health services. According to the Mental Health Commission and various national reports, waiting times for counselling can extend to months in many areas. This delay disproportionately affects vulnerable individuals, particularly those experiencing mild to moderate mental health challenges such as anxiety, depression, grief, trauma, the impacts of addiction, and relationship issues. Each client is assessed by our skilled clinical team prior to being placed with a volunteer counsellor, who provides them with up to 24 counselling sessions over a 6 month period on the same day and time each week.
Access to counselling…
innovations.desc:
Living Life Counselling was established to serve:
- Individuals who cannot afford private therapy (often €60–€100 per session)
- People experiencing social exclusion or economic disadvantage
- Those in urgent need of emotional support, directed towards us by health care professionals and public health services, who may be ineligible for acute care or are unable to avail of these services due to long wait lists.
- Our catchment area covers all of County Wicklow, up to and including the Wicklow/Wexford border, as well as Southeast County Dublin.
Model of Operation
Living Life Counselling operates a low-cost, donation-based counselling model, offering a professional service with no fixed fee, instead encouraging clients to contribute what they can afford.

innovations.name: Cohousing Bellefleur
innovations.problem:
The Bellefleur project addresses several key urban and social challenges in the Belgian context.
About the Belgian housing context:
1. Financing Barriers One of the main challenges is access to affordable financing. Belgian banks remain hesitant to support cooperative housing. Currently, wooncoop can secure only 35–40% loan-to-value financing, often at interest rates 1% higher than those offered to individual homebuyers. Moreover, individuals are not allowed to take out a bank loan to buy shares in a housing cooperative, which limits broader participation.
If housing cooperatives were treated equally to individual homeowners in financial terms, cooperative living would becomee even more…
innovations.desc:
1. Housing Insecurity & Affordability Problem. Solution: Because of wooncoop's coöperative housing system people with not a lot of means can still live at Bellfleur and enjoy the benefits of owing a house. Next to that Bellefleur includes a solidarity apartment for residents with lower incomes, funded by the community and wooncoop investors, making quality housing accessible to more people.

innovations.name: UNFOLDING THE COMPLEX PATTERNS IN PEOPLE-PLACE RELATIONSHIP
innovations.problem: Today, it can be tough for local governments and stakeholders to address the needs of city residents and channel their voices into urban development. This is particularly true in smaller cities in the peripheral regions of the European Union. Our urban research, driven by social innovation, seeks to create a comprehensive approach that combines insights from urban studies and environmental psychology. This approach can help decision-makers create lasting policy solutions and empower local communities to use their resources.
innovations.desc: Our research involves several key steps: identifying the city's spatial and governing characteristics, analysing the municipality's socio-economic data from the central statistical office’s database, and conducting quantitative and qualitative analyses. The quantitative analysis includes sociodemographic and socioeconomic questions, assessing the settlement's connotative meaning, satisfaction scales to measure overall well-being, and evaluating the perceived attractiveness of certain urban characteristics, as well as exploring latent attitudes like place attachment and identity. The qualitative analysis involves semi-structured focus group interviews with local stakeholders to understand their ‘sensing’ of the city. Additionally, we'll observe people's behaviour in public spaces to better understand how they interact with the city.
innovations.target: Long-term or repeatedly unemployed persons, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Other target groups

Our analysis reveals individuals' relationships with specific urban locations, providing valuable tools for examining the complex interactions between people and places, thereby enhancing the city's livability and responsiveness to future challenges. innovations.desc: The aim of the research is to identify the traits, entrepreneurial competences, entrepreneurial attitudes, entrepreneurial motivations, entrepreneurial behaviours, entrepreneurial characteristics that determine who becomes a successful entrepreneur throughout life, or who fails at the early stages of entrepreneurial life. One of these actions has facilitated the creation of the European Platform on Combating Homelessness (EPOCH), to which the 27 Member States have signed up to end homelessness by 2030. One of the recommendations put forward for this purpose is using…

innovations.name: Social Innovation and Common goods, a path for young entrepreneurs
innovations.problem: Young people in Europe, particularly in Italy and Spain, face high youth unemployment, limited access to entrepreneurial education, and a lack of opportunities to engage in socially and environmentally responsible economic activities. Existing training and support systems often fail to integrate values such as social justice, sustainability, and community well-being, leaving a gap between young people’s aspirations and the tools available to realize them. This disconnect contributes to underutilized potential among youth and limits their role in shaping a more inclusive and sustainable economy.
innovations.desc:
The project offers a unique cross-border training and mentoring pathway that blends social innovation practices with the Economy of the Common Good framework—an approach rarely integrated into youth entrepreneurship programs. It combines online learning, expert guidance, and peer collaboration to foster ethical, sustainable business development. By engaging youth in a participatory, values-based learning environment and connecting them with real-life practitioners, the project equips them with both the technical skills and the social mindset needed to launch impactful ventures that prioritize people and planet alongside profit.
This project draws inspiration from the Economy of the Common Good (ECG) movement, originating in Austria, which promotes sustainable and socially responsible business models prioritizing human dignity, ecological sustainability, and democratic participation. It…
innovations.target: NEETs (Not in Education, Employment, or Training), Individuals experiencing gender marginalization
innovations.evidence: 40 young participants (ages 23–27) trained in social innovation and sustainable entrepreneurship. 10 video lessons produced and made available online for wider dissemination and long-term use. 20 mentors and experts involved in delivering tailored support and real-world insights. 2 international study visits promoting cross-cultural exchange and practical learning. Increased employability and entrepreneurial readiness among youth, with a focus on ethical and community-oriented ventures. Strengthened collaboration between organizations in Italy and Spain, building a transnational ecosystem for…

innovations.name: Social entrepreneurship for Roma
innovations.problem: The project addressed multiple interlinked challenges affecting both Roma communities and the functioning of social enterprises. Members of the Roma community, particularly the long-term unemployed and recipients of social assistance, often face social exclusion, limited access to quality education and training, and significant barriers to entering the labour market. At the same time, existing staff in social enterprises lacked sufficient training in key areas such as administration, management, and marketing, which hindered the sustainability and growth of such enterprises. There was also a lack of structured mentorship and support for Roma individuals to develop and implement business…
innovations.desc: The project stood out for its integrated and inclusive approach to social entrepreneurship, combining capacity-building for both employed staff and members of the Roma community. Its innovation lay in offering parallel, tailored mentorship programs—one for employees of the social enterprise to strengthen managerial, administrative, and marketing competencies, and another for Roma participants focused on developing entrepreneurial skills and understanding cooperatives. By supporting Roma individuals in shaping concrete business ideas and guiding them through the process of creating business plans, the project bridged the gap between social inclusion and economic empowerment. Additionally, the project introduced social entrepreneurship not just as a skillset, but as a pathway to sustainable employment and community development, helping to reframe perceptions of Roma communities through…
innovations.target: Migrants and ethnic minorities, Long-term or repeatedly unemployed persons
innovations.benef: EPEKA: Scientific and Research Association for Art, Cultural and Educational Programmes and Technology
innovations.evidence: The project brought a range of impactful results and lasting benefits. At the same time, ten members of the Roma community participated in a comprehensive 225-hour programme focused on social entrepreneurship, innovation, and cooperative models. This helped them gain practical knowledge and the confidence to develop business ideas, which were further supported through guidance in drafting concrete…

innovations.name: ENHANCE – ENHancing Adult learNers voiCEs
innovations.problem: Adult learners—especially those facing gender, racial, social, and economic exclusion—are systemically excluded from influencing the very learning systems designed to support them. This results in disconnected policy, tokenistic inclusion, and missed opportunities for transformative social innovation.
innovations.desc:
ENHANCE flips the system: it centers adult learners as co-creators of education. By weaving together a European matrix of critically understanding existing practices, developing participatory tools like the Learners’ Voices Roadmap, and integrating learner-led storytelling and podcasts in public life, the project shifts ALE (Adult Learning and Education) from top-down provision to collective empowerment.
The ENHANCE project draws inspiration from AONTAS’s “Community Education Network” (CEN) in Ireland, a nationally recognized approach in the adult learning and education sector. The CEN has long advocated for the inclusion of learners' voices in shaping education policy and practice, with a focus on empowering marginalized communities through learner-led consultation processes and public engagement campaigns, such as the “Learners as Leaders” initiative. This Irish model demonstrated how…
innovations.target: Migrants and ethnic minorities, Individuals experiencing gender marginalization, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.benef: European Associaton for the Education of Adults
innovations.evidence: A transnational matrix of learners’ voice initiatives A Learners' Voice Roadmap and policy recommendations targeting education stakeholders and decision-makers A podcast series publicly reclaiming space for learners’ stories Increased civic and democratic participation of adult learners, particularly in relation to the 2024 EU elections Strengthened policy engagement capacities of ALE organisations and learners
authors: European Associaton for the Education of Adults

innovations.name: Integration through Sport project
innovations.problem: Many new migrant communities have limited social connections and face cultural and language barriers. Partaking in sporting activities can build their sense of belonging, language skills, and inter cultural friendships. Often newcomers live in accommodation centres across the city and lack connections within the communities they reside.  In addition, we found that many  children attended school across the city and had no connection with local communities within which they were living.
innovations.desc: By targeting the already existing sporting infrastructure, it meant that the sports clubs that agreed to come on board with our Integration though sport project were supported to actively target children and adults that were living in accommodation centres in their area and support and encourage their participation at a local level.
innovations.target: Migrants and ethnic minorities
innovations.benef: Limerick City Area Partnership (formally PAUL Partnership)
innovations.evidence: The results have been very positive and  involved children and adults becoming actively involved in their local clubs. This project allowed social networks to develop among parents, it allowed children to develop and establish friendships within their local areas, and gave them a sense of belonging.  It has enabled and facilitated the development of social capital for members of migrant communities.
authors: Limerick City Area Partnership (formally PAUL Partnership)

innovations.name: Tracking What Matters: A data framework to drive decisions and prove long-term impact
innovations.problem: Every year, billions of euros are invested in skills development across the EU, with €30–35 billion allocated to vocational training in France, ~€30 billion in Spain, ~€25 billion in Italy, and ~€42 billion in the UK. Additionally, for the 2021–2027 period, the European Social Fund Plus (ESF+) has allocated €40.4 billion for skills development, with total investments in skills under EU cohesion funds reaching €67.7 billion. However, despite this massive financial commitment, there remains limited evidence on the long-term impact of VET programs. Where evidence does exist, it is often fragmented or inconclusive, making it difficult to identify what works, for whom, and under which…
innovations.desc: Generation’s innovative solution lies in our comprehensive, multi-year learner data tracking system - one of the most extensive in the VET space globally. At the heart of our approach is a firm belief that true impact must be measured not only by how many people we serve (breadth), but also by how deeply and sustainably our programs transform lives (depth and durability). While many training providers focus on short-term outputs like graduation or initial placement, Generation systematically tracks learner outcomes for up to five years post-programme—something few, if any, VET providers do at this scale and granularity. Our data framework follows each learner across their full journey, from application to long-term career growth, capturing detailed, real-time insights across multiple dimensions: employment status, wage evolution, promotion rates, financial resilience, mental and…
innovations.target: Long-term or repeatedly unemployed persons, NEETs (Not in Education, Employment, or Training), Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence: Generation’s data-driven system has led to significant results and measurable benefits at all levels of our work, enabling us to deliver higher quality training, respond quickly to emerging challenges, and enhance the overall impact of the resources we deploy. Our extensive suite of operational dashboards allows us to monitor and respond to programme performance in real time. These dashboards, covering areas such as recruitment, learner experience, instructor and mentor performance, placement rates, and alumni outcomes, are central to our ability to quickly diagnose problems and adjust our…

innovations.name: From farm to fork: a social chain of food aid
innovations.problem: This project adresses the difficulties to access to diversified and high-quality food for the most deprived populations. Also, as part of this project, the beneficiaries have access to the "Nourishing food" training in order to learn and share practices.

No one is left behind: from the farmers in social and professional insertion, the volunteer and the coordinators that are trained as part of this project to the beneficiaries, everyone is part of this economy and can find an essential place.

At first, only few gardens and food banks were sollicited. It doubled the next year.
Today, this social chain of food aid means 420 tonnes of fruits and vegetables exchanged between 52 gardens and 38 food banks this last year. It’s 2,995 farmers involved for roughly 1,455,271 beneficiaries.

innovations.name: Driving License for Independent Living program
innovations.problem: Homelessness has increased by 70% across the EU in the past decade. It is one of the most severe forms of poverty, stemming from a complex mix of structural, institutional, and individual factors. According to the European Parliament (2020), member states should decriminalize homelessness and ensure equal access to essential public services such as healthcare, education, and social welfare. For young people, independence means learning to live responsibly and manage everyday life. This includes forming an identity, handling financial insecurity, establishing routines, and maintaining a home. Neuropsychiatric conditions, mental health challenges, or substance use issues can make these tasks…
innovations.desc: In Finland, homelessness prevention has not been addressed in this way before. We have developed a low-threshold coaching model that has proven effective. It is a preventive method that allows us to measure both impact and outcomes. Our training program is built around peer support and experiential learning. It consists of the following modules: 1.The Meaning of Home Participants reflect on why a home is important and what kinds of emotions and memories are connected to it. 2.Tenant Rights and Responsibilities This module introduces tenant rights, such as those related to renovations, rental agreements, and fair housing practices. It also covers important responsibilities like following house rules and maintaining the home. 3.Maintaining a Home and Housing Safety Participants learn how to keep their home clean and in good condition, and how to ensure fire safety and other basic living…
innovations.target: Migrants and ethnic minorities, Homeless persons, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence: The Driving License for Independent Living program has reached a total of 754 people in need of support through group coaching, one-on-one sessions, and online training. Of those participants, 97 percent reported improved housing skills. Additionally, 89 percent of those who completed the training continued living in their homes without disturbances, warnings, evictions or rent arrears. Through the program, 15 people experiencing long-term homelessness have found permanent housing. All of them, 100 percent, succeeded in maintaining their housing over a one-year follow-up period. The program…

innovations.name: Holistic approach of accompanying measures and services for people living below the poverty line in West Athens within the FEAD framework.
innovations.problem: West Athens is a large area with a population that faces common problems. Until now, social services have been provided at the local level by the Municipalities. In particular, poverty in West Athens is a persistent reality and ensuring basic needs such as food, shelter, education and access to health services is becoming difficult. The available resources such as FEAD would not be enough if the actions were planned separately in each Municipality and could not cover so many and different needs of the beneficiaries.
innovations.desc: The way in which the social inclusion accompanying services were provided to the beneficiaries of a large area of action (West Athens - 8 Municipalities) through inter-municipal cooperation of social services. Also, the organization of the Project in stages as well as the provision of services that came to satisfy the specific and diagnosed needs of the beneficiaries themselves who chose it.

innovations.name: The Library of Things
innovations.problem: In many communities, access to educational, creative, and sensory tools remains a privilege — limited by financial constraints, lack of space, or systemic inequality. Families with lower income, educators with scarce resources, and individuals with special needs, particularly neurodiverse children, often cannot afford items that support learning, emotional regulation, or self-expression. Essential tools such as sensory equipment, Montessori materials, or musical instruments are often out of reach for those who need them most. Moreover, many valuable items are underused or discarded due to infrequent need, contributing to waste and unsustainable consumption patterns. Public institutions…
innovations.desc: The Library of Things reimagines the role of a public library as a socially innovative platform that offers not only access to information but also to physical resources essential for learning, creativity, and well-being. As the first initiative of its kind in Lithuania and the Baltic region, it transforms traditional library services by allowing users to borrow over 200 items — from sensory tools and educational games to musical instruments and exploration tools such as microscopes and telescopes — entirely free of charge. What makes this solution innovative is its holistic and inclusive design: 1) It directly supports neurodiverse users, families, and educators by providing access to high-quality tools that would otherwise be unaffordable. 2) It includes instructional videos and printed guides for effective use, particularly for parents of children with special needs. 3) It leverages…
innovations.target: Individuals with disabilities, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised
innovations.benef: Šiauliai County Povilas Višinskis Public Library
innovations.evidence: Since its launch, the Library of Things has demonstrated a clear and growing need within the community. Over 1,300 residents have already used the service, with many items in constant circulation and waiting lists extending for several months. This sustained demand highlights not only the practical value of the collection but also its role in supporting inclusive education, creativity, and well-being. Importantly, the initiative has succeeded in engaging new user groups who do not typically visit libraries, thereby broadening cultural participation and strengthening social inclusion. It…

Specifically, the project tackles: • Lack of Access to the Creative Process: Traditionally, accessibility initiatives have focused on making existing images accessible to people with visual disabilities (e.g., through tactile reproductions or descriptions). innovations.name: Mind The Gap
innovations.problem: The project has tackled the widespread social and economic exclusion of NEETs (young people not in education, employment or training) in Italy’s Campania Region. The area suffers a combination of early high school leaving, low educational outcomes, and persistent youth unemployment—conditions that leave many young people without the skills, support, or confidence to access training or work. Many NEETs face serious challenges: educational systems often fail to engage them meaningfully or provide the competencies required by today’s labour market. At the same time, material poverty, limited access to services, and a lack of motivation have deepened their sense of isolation and hopelessness.…
innovations.desc: The project has tackled these urgent challenges by offering vulnerable NEETs a structured, empowering pathway back into active life. Through tailored guidance, hands-on training, and a meaningful transnational mobility experience, the initiative not only has developed market-relevant skills but has also restored self-confidence, motivation, and hope. One of the project’s most innovative aspects has been the integration of the ALMA scheme into existing professional training pathways, such as those for chefs, pizza or pastry makers. This approach was complemented by additional support measures, including psychological counseling and career orientation services. These combined elements were designed to maximize the already highly positive impact of these training courses on employability and make them truly effective for the NEET target group. Furthermore, the  project has promoted…

Despite their enthusiasm, students also reported some concerns.
