BIP/ZIP projects are encouraged to search for other funding sources, such as sponsorship from local enterprises. The BIP/ZIP programme strives to include…
innovations.benef: Housing and Local Development municipal department of the city of Lisbon
innovations.evidence: By 2019, the programme had funded almost 2 000 local initiatives in 67 BIP/ZIP territories in Lisbon. In total, one fifth of the Lisbon population has participated in the programme, and approximately EUR 12.4 million has funded more than 300 city-wide projects. 610 organisations have participated in BIP/ZIP projects to date. The main beneficiaries of the programme have been local communities who benefit from support and funding for projects that foster inclusion and social cohesion, employment and education. More than 150 private companies, NGOs and local government authorities are a part of…
authors: Housing and Local Development municipal department of the city of Lisbon

innovations.name: Cleanup day
innovations.problem: The volume of litter in our environment is growing. Our mobile lifestyles have increased the risk of people deliberately or accidentally discarding litter in both urban and rural environments, instead of disposing of it responsibly using the established waste management systems. This has a grave impact, both environmentally and financially. The financial costs associated with cleaning up litter are high. The Clean Europe Network estimates that cleaning up all the current land litter across the European Union could cost around EUR 13 billion .
innovations.desc:
The Let’s Do It Foundation organised a national ‘Cleanup Day’ in Estonia to help manage litter in the country by actively engaging citizens to do their part in protecting the environment. The Cleanup Day was crowd-sourced and organised in cooperation with over 500 organisations, from NGOs and public authorities to private companies and IT specialists. The latter were involved in creating an app to map illegal waste locations by enabling citizens themselves to mark locations as they were cleaning litter. The day was promoted through a large, nation-wide communication campaign supported by prominent Estonians and international media coverage.
This innovative solution of involving citizens and organisations in cleaning up litter across the country quickly gained popularity in other countries. The initiative, continually supported by the Let’s Do it Foundation, became global in the form of…
innovations.evidence:
During the Estonian Cleanup day, 4% of the total Estonian population collected 10 000 tonnes of garbage. The high turnout demonstrated citizen engagement and successful citizen-led action. It gave the impetus for the Let’s Do It Foundation’s other social and environmental activities. The first cleanup was also deemed extremely efficient, as it was completed in five hours with a budget of EUR 500 000. According to official estimations , the government would have spent more than three years and around EUR 22.5 million to achieve a similar result. [1]
The World Cleanup Day, organised on 15…

innovations.name: Look after my parents
innovations.problem: The elderly are at a higher risk of experiencing loneliness and suffering from social isolation than other age groups. This can have negative impacts on their physical and mental wellbeing , including anxiety, depression and intense feelings of vulnerability. Around 6 million people in France are over the age of 75. Of these, one in four lives alone. 300 000 people over the age of 60 are in a situation of social isolation, rarely or never meeting other people from all of their social networks combined (i.e. family, friends, neighbourhood, community network).
innovations.desc:
Look after my parents ( Veiller sur mes parents ) is a service, developed by La Poste in 2017, that aims to tackle the social isolation of elderly people through regular social visits from mail delivery staff. La Poste is the largest mail delivery service in France and operates across the country. It has a unique ability to reach individuals in all parts of France, including those in more remote locations. Look after my parents is innovative in that it takes this regular, mainstream service and transforms it into an effective outreach and support service for the most vulnerable.
Service users can select from a range of packages. The most popular is a weekly visit to the elderly individual by the mail carrier. The service relies on an app, which allows the mail carrier to send a short report back to the elderly person’s relatives, or other nominated contacts, keeping the family updated…
innovations.evidence:
Around 40 000 mail carriers were trained before launching the service. The results achieved by October 2019 show that around 7 500 elderly people were using the services, and of these 6 000 were women. The clients’ average age was 82. The visits usually lasted between six and fifteen minutes.
The initiative, however, has been met with some concerns from certain groups, including the La Poste trade union, as they feel that the service commercialises social relations. Furthermore, there is a risk that mail carriers do not have the adequate expertise to provide the service, which may involve…

innovations.name: HomeLab
innovations.problem: Homelessness, poverty, and a lack of work opportunities are interlinked problems, experienced across four Central and Eastern European countries (CEE) (Czechia, Hungary, Poland, and Slovakia). Sudden and substantial structural changes and privatisation of the housing market over the last two decades have resulted in poor housing security and limited social accommodation in these countries. The share of households that suffer from severe housing deprivation was 11.7% in these four Member States in 2017 , significantly higher than the EU average (5%).
innovations.desc:
HomeLab aimed to support vulnerable households out of their precarious circumstances by helping them to find suitable and affordable housing, simultaneously boosting their employment and social prospects. HomeLab ran from 2016 to 2019 through five pilot projects in Czechia, Hungary, Poland, and Slovakia, with two pilots in Hungary. The project is based on the innovative Social Rental Enterprise (SRE) model, which asserts that housing and employment problems must be tackled simultaneously. HomeLab provided its service users - individuals excluded from mainstream social services - with frequent follow-ups and strong personal support. This model of providing a number of interlinked social services is innovative and unique, as it marks a shift towards an individual, people-centred approach to tackling complex social issues.
The project was coordinated by the Hungarian Metropolitan Research…
innovations.target: Homeless persons, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised
innovations.benef: Metropolitan Research Institute, Romodrom o.p.s., People in Need Slovakia, Habitat for Humanity Poland, Hungarian Charity Service of the Order of Malta, From Street to Home (Utcáról Lakásba Egyesület), Budapest Institute
innovations.evidence: The monitoring and evaluation activities of the project found that the integrated service provision led to significant improvement in the housing conditions of participants in the pilot projects. Changes in the employment positions of HomeLab clients (compared to the control group) were more varied, but overall significant improvement was registered. HomeLab particularly improved the employment status of both those with inadequate housing, and also vulnerable labour market positions, having less of an impact on those who began in a relatively more stable position. Employment impacts were…
authors: Metropolitan Research Institute, Romodrom o.p.s., People in Need Slovakia, Habitat for Humanity Poland, Hungarian Charity Service of the Order of Malta, From Street to Home (Utcáról Lakásba Egyesület), Budapest Institute

innovations.name: Eco-Schools
innovations.problem: The vast majority of Europeans highly value the protection of the environment and are aware of the challenges related to environmental sustainability. However, households in the European Union produce high levels of municipal waste, adding up to 492 kg per person . This illustrates the need to further promote more sustainable habits among European citizens. These habits can be fostered and developed through education.
innovations.desc:
Eco-Schools is a global education programme that teaches children about pressing and urgent environmental problems in school. The Eco-Schools programme is the largest global programme implemented in schools that tackles sustainable and environmental issues. The Eco-Schools philosophy is to build on the existing schooling system to deliver a curriculum that covers the environment and sustainable development, using participatory methodologies to empower and inspire pupils.
The concept originated in Germany, Greece, and the United Kingdom in 1994 and was gradually transferred to other countries. The global programme is managed by the Foundation for Environmental Education (FEE) which is headquartered in Copenhagen, Denmark. This programme is especially wide-reaching in Latvia, as it is the most comprehensive nation-wide school programme on environmental issues.
The programme taps into the…
innovations.evidence: In Latvia, the Eco-Schools programme involves around 20 000 students through more than 200 educational institutions, ranging from primary to higher education. These results represent a success for a country of fewer than 2 million citizens. In 2018, the Eco-Schools Summer Forum brought together 120 teachers from 70 Eco-Schools and more than 100 students. The event’s popularity as a longstanding tradition and the positive experiences of it reported by students and teachers demonstrate the importance of the programme in raising awareness of sustainability among children and the wider…

innovations.name: Food and people (ended)
innovations.problem: In rural Denmark, the farming community is diminishing, as local farmers who have been impacted by globalisation cannot afford to scale-up their food production and distribution on their own. The Danish food production sector is very industrialised and centralised, and opportunities for processing farming commodities locally are limited. Under legislation governing food safety, it is not profitable for farmers to establish their own processing facilities, leading to a diminishing farming sector and a rural population facing unemployment and skills depletion.
innovations.desc:
Food and People is a social enterprise that promotes sustainable growth and the development of new and established local micro enterprises. It does so by giving farmers access to communal processing facilities, whilst offering skills training and flexible job opportunities to vulnerable individuals, including people with disabilities.
Local farmers can use Food and People’s communal processing facilities for handling, processing, storing and distributing their own produce. Its facilities for food production are situated in a renovated, previously unused agricultural building on Grønnessegaard Manor, an estate in rural Denmark. The facilities comply with European standards for food safety. Farmers can sell their products through the farm shop at the Manor, and food produced through the communal processing facilities is also used for catering, including the delivery of food to local…
innovations.target: Other target groups
innovations.evidence: Access of farmers to the communal processing facilities and to the web shop and showroom to sell local products have facilitated food production and sale and, in turn, boosted the local economy. Farmers have also learned how to adhere to European standards of food safety when handling, processing, storing and distributing their products. The project has allowed for the development, marketing, processing and distribution of two innovative, locally-sourced products – the Halsnæs food box and the Halsnæs Christmas box, which are publicised and marketed on the web shop and showroom, further…

innovations.name: ResQ Club
innovations.problem: Around 88 million tonnes of food is wasted annually in the European Union. In Finland alone, approximately 120–160 million kilograms of food is wasted by households (about 20–25 kilogrammes per person).  This waste costs the EU an estimated EUR 143 million and has significant negative effects on the environment, as food waste depletes the world of finite natural resources, such as water, and contributes to global warming.
innovations.desc:
The Finnish start-up ResQ Club has developed a location-based mobile app that enables consumers to buy surplus food that would otherwise be thrown away by restaurants, cafes, hotels and grocery stores. The food is discounted from 30% up to 100%. The chosen food product can be bought through the app using a payment card or PayPal. Once the transaction has gone through, the consumer is able to pick up the meal whenever they want from a pick-up window set by the supplier, and without having to wait. Restaurants, cafes, and grocery stores can sign up to ResQ Club through the online platform, where they can announce their surplus products and meals. ResQ Club’s overall goal is to limit the amount of food that goes to waste in restaurants to zero.
ResQ adopts a franchising model, but also operates some market areas itself. Its management remains centralised in Finland. All the profits made by…
innovations.evidence: The benefits of this initiative extend both to restaurants and customers. Consumers are able to buy food that is close to its expiry date, at a reduced price. Restaurants, cafes and grocery stores are able to sell food that would otherwise go to waste. Latest figures show that the app has over 30 000 active monthly users and sells around 80 000 portions of food each month in the cities where ResQ Club is active . The app has been downloaded 800 000 times. A total of 7 000 restaurants, cafes and grocery stores have so far registered on the app, and about 1 300 of them sell food through the…

innovations.name: Cooperative for Ethical Financing (ZEF)
innovations.problem: Since the 2008 economic and financial crisis, there has been heightened interest in socially responsible finance and ethical banking. This is in part due to a lack of confidence in traditional banks caused by the high number of bailouts in the aftermath of the crisis. Additionally, as environmental awareness is rising, people are turning away from traditional banking, which can cause environmental damage through investment in unsustainable development .
innovations.desc: The Cooperative for Ethical Financing (ZEF) is a non-profit organisation based in Croatia, which aims to provide ethical banking alternatives for consumers. ZEF, created in 2014, is the first ethical banking cooperative in Croatia, and uses traditional financial tools to achieve ethical results. ZEF offers a variety of financial instruments to its members, including micro loans for social entrepreneurs, pre-financing for local action groups, and accounting services for cooperatives. By becoming members of the cooperative, individuals and organisations join the market created by ZEF. Members can manage their finances in a way that has a positive social and environmental impact. They can take out loans, crowdfund other members and invest in other members’ projects. Members can also benefit from non-financial services, such as access to business and financial consulting, as well as…
innovations.evidence:
Overall, ZEF’s impact has been far-reaching, as demonstrated by the fact that it has become the largest cooperative in Croatia, with 1 300 members at present. The combined revenue from the sale of ZEF members’ goods and services exceeds EUR 250 million per year.
According to Goran Jeras, the Cooperative Manager, the main achievement of ZEF has been ‘the creation of an extremely diverse range of participants’, where people from all over the country, with different political views and religious backgrounds, come together to benefit the community through ethical financing. Jeras explains that…

innovations.name: AfB - Social and green IT
innovations.problem: People with disabilities can face multiple obstacles to entering the workplace, often due to stigma or a scarcity of inclusive job positions that can be adapted to their individual abilities. In 2017, there were 7.7 million people of working age with a severe disability in Germany. The disability pay gap and a lack of information about vacancies reduce the chance of people with disabilities finding quality employment. Employers are also sometimes not confident that they will be able to support an employee with a disability and provide them with a barrier-free workspace, and thus do not provide many opportunities for people with disabilities.
innovations.desc:
AfB is a social enterprise that aims to create inclusive, barrier-free jobs in refurbishing and reselling used IT hardware. Its innovation lies in its ability to support people with disabilities in their search for employment and to raise awareness amongst employers on disability issues, whilst also helping to reduce the negative environmental impact of IT production and waste. It aims to become one of the leading non-profit IT companies worldwide.
AfB is based on a socially responsible business model sustained by its partnership with over 1 000 corporations, banks and public institutions. AfB collects used IT and mobile hardware, repairs it, certifiably removes stored data, and resells it at a reduced price in AfB stores or online. AfB subsequently provides each partner organisation with a certificate of Corporate Social Responsibility, in which the social and environmental impact of…
innovations.evidence:
As a result of AfB’s inclusive employment strategy, the company has around 440 employees in 19 different locations, of which approximately half have a disability. Employees are supported by social workers, as well as a representative in the case of severely disabled people. The company has experienced rapid growth over recent years, with 63 employees hired in 2019 alone.
In 2019, AfB processed more than 470 000 pieces of IT equipment and mobile devices, of which 65% were refurbished. It contributed to savings of around 52 300 megawatt hours of energy, 17 000 tonnes of CO2 emissions and 22 900…

innovations.name: SIMPACT
innovations.problem: Methods for measuring the economic impact of social innovation and for finding out which business models are best for sustaining social innovation have not been fully defined, due to a lack of empirical research. This gap hinders the ability of both policy makers and businesses to ensure impactful social innovation, and to mainstream socially innovative practices into the European economic and policy environment.
innovations.desc:
SIMPACT is a collaborative research project involving 12 partners across ten European countries. It aims to promote social innovation targeting vulnerable and marginalised groups by understanding its economic dimensions. SIMPACT is based on the understanding that social innovation involves a broader range of groups than traditional innovation, and that all have valuable experience in what does and does not work. Based on this philosophy, the project involves a wide range of social innovation stakeholders in its research and work – in particular, vulnerable groups who are the end beneficiaries of actions.
SIMPACT combines theoretical research and empirical evidence with continuous stakeholder dialogue at all levels. Small-scale stakeholder experiments with marginalised and vulnerable groups are used to test findings and tools – ‘indicator labs’, for example, involve representatives of…
innovations.target: Migrants and ethnic minorities, Long-term or repeatedly unemployed persons
innovations.benef: IAT, The Centre for Social Research (TUDO), The Social Innovation Centre - SINNERGIAK (SIN), The CIS (former Centre of Economic Studies), The Netherlands Organisation of Applied Scientific Research (TNO), The Maastricht Economic & Social Research Institute on Innovation and Technology (UM-MERIT), Politecnico di Milano (POLIMI), NEOMA Business School, The Centre for European Policy Studies (CEPS), NORDREGIO, The Karelian Institute
innovations.evidence:
The active multi-level participation approach was employed from the very beginning of the project and has consistently supported the translation of research findings into practice. From 2014 to 2016, the project engaged a variety of stakeholders, including unemployed young people, migrants, older people, social innovators, policy makers and statisticians, all of whom contributed to the development of three toolboxes.
The SI Business Toolbox helps social investors or social innovators to develop, measure and assess social innovation, and the SI Impact Assessment Toolbox is a practical guide…
authors: IAT, The Centre for Social Research (TUDO), The Social Innovation Centre - SINNERGIAK (SIN), The CIS (former Centre of Economic Studies), The Netherlands Organisation of Applied Scientific Research (TNO), The Maastricht Economic & Social Research Institute on Innovation and Technology (UM-MERIT), Politecnico di Milano (POLIMI), NEOMA Business School, The Centre for European Policy Studies (CEPS), NORDREGIO, The Karelian Institute

innovations.name: Halandri Parents Social Cooperative
innovations.problem: The economic and financial crisis has had a grave impact on public spending in Greece, with large cuts in funding for social services and education. In the northern Athenian suburb of Halandri, five of the nine municipal kindergartens closed down in 2011, leaving over 50 people without work, and the parents of 2 000 pre-school age children with very few childcare options. At the same time, high schools faced cuts, which increased class sizes and negatively affected the quality of teaching.
innovations.desc:
The Halandri Parents Social Cooperative Enterprise was founded by a committee of parents in 2012. It aims to fill the gaps in public services by empowering and mobilising community members to drive solutions themselves. Through its cooperative model, it responds directly to changing childcare and education needs in the local area, through several initiatives based on one principle – profit-free quality childcare and education that puts the learning of the pupil first.
The cooperative started with a childcare programme in 2012, setting up small schools in private homes to meet the demand for affordable childcare in the area. The programme relies on parent volunteers to keep fees low. In 2013, the cooperative expanded to set up a school of private tuition, which offers classes to high school students preparing for university exams at affordable rates.
The school uses modern educational…
innovations.benef: Halandri Parents Social Cooperative Enterprise, Margarita Vocational Training Centre
innovations.evidence:
The cooperative employs four full-time paid employees, eight part-time paid employees and ten volunteers. The childcare facility accommodates over 20 children from the neighbourhood.
One of the key benefits of the cooperative is that it has been able to set up additional activities addressing emerging problems in the community. In addition to childcare and private tuition, for example, it set up a parent group coaching programme, which aims to raise public awareness, foster the exchange of opinions, and educate parents and adolescents on a series of general and specialised parenting…
authors: Halandri Parents Social Cooperative Enterprise, Margarita Vocational Training Centre

innovations.name: Impact Hub Athens
innovations.problem:
In recent years, there has been a growing interest in social entrepreneurship across Europe, driven by factors such as economic crises and a collective desire for more inclusive and sustainable economic systems. Social enterprises play a pivotal role in addressing societal challenges, promoting social inclusion, and fostering sustainable development. However, the support structures available to social entrepreneurs—encompassing funding opportunities, capacity building, and knowledge sharing—vary significantly across European countries. In many regions, support remains limited or fragmented, hindering the growth and scalability of social enterprises.​
To address these disparities, the…
innovations.desc:
Impact Hub Athens addresses the absence of structural support for social entrepreneurs by tapping into the unused potential of international networking and knowledge sharing.  Impact Hub is the first global collaborative network of its kind, designed specifically to support and connect social entrepreneurs across the globe, whilst also providing them with co-working space. Membership packages for social entrepreneurs range from EUR 18.00 to EUR 170.00. Membership gives individuals access to both a physical workspace, a vibrant multi-disciplinary community, and a range of services to support them at different stages of their enterprise development.
Impact Hub Athens supports entrepreneurs working in the fields of urbanism, active citizenship, the circular economy, the environment and systemic change for social integration. Its business incubator provides training on capacity building,…
innovations.target: Other target groups
innovations.evidence:
Over the past 10 years, Impact Hub Athens has supported more than 300 social and environmental ventures , trained over 3,000 individuals in entrepreneurship and upskilling, and built a community of over 1,000 members and partners . These social innovators are part of the broader Impact Hub global network, contributing to a culture of collaboration by sharing expertise and co-developing solutions across borders.
Run by a team of 12 full-time experts —including trainers, facilitators, programme managers, researchers, and community builders—Impact Hub Athens hosts a 750 sqm innovation space in…

innovations.name: Bio-Village Seeham
innovations.problem: Global emissions from crop and livestock agriculture rose by 16% from 2000 to 2017 . In the EU, 40% of agricultural emissions are nitrous oxide, in part produced by the use of nitrogen fertilisers in conventional farming. Organic farming has been developed as a response to the environmental harm caused by the use of chemical pesticides and synthetic fertilisers in conventional agriculture. It has ecological benefits, in that it can contribute to a more sustainable and environmentally friendly food production system.
innovations.desc:
Bio-Village Seeham is the first organic village in Austria that focuses on maintaining and preserving traditional methods of haymaking and organic farming. In 2011, as interest in environmentally friendly lifestyles started to increase, the Seeham municipality began to collaborate with local citizens, farmers and businesses, creating the Bio-Village. The Bio-Village aims to preserve the traditional production of hay milk produced from feeding cows hay and grass mixed with natural herbs, which accounts for only 0.3% of milk produced in the EU. Through this, the Bio-Village promotes community and an environmentally friendly lifestyle, and helps to boost the local economy.
The Bio-Village is a community of local farmers, citizens and businesses. It runs a range of projects, including an organic food store, a flower festival, a community garden, the provision of organic fresh food to school…
innovations.evidence: In addition to preserving the traditional method of haymaking and its positive effects on the environment, the Bio-Village has generated a number of benefits. Local farmers and producers benefit, as they are able to sell their high-quality products such as milk, honey, wax, dairy products, juice and herbs, at a higher price. Local citizens benefit from food and products that are 100% organic and can attend social community events. Tourists and visitors benefit from the local hospitality, organic products and healthy lifestyle, and can learn more about organic farming and hay milk…

innovations.name: Visits in the Dark
innovations.problem: Visually impaired people often struggle to find employment due to a lack of accessible job opportunities. In 2013, there were approximately 102 000 visually impaired people in Czechia, which was around 6% of the population with disabilities. The employment rate of people with any type of disability in 2013 was around 47%.
innovations.desc:
Visits in the Dark employs visually impaired people to visit elderly people for 1.5 hours a week. The innovation of the project is the way that it redesigns social support typically provided to visually impaired people, who are normally passive recipients of state support. The project empowers them to become active contributors to society, whilst increasing their skills and autonomy.
The project was set up in 2017 by the Czech Radio Endowment Fund, which has 18 years of experience in working with visually impaired people. To become an employee – a ‘visitor’ – a visually impaired person must have an interest in working with elderly people, have a hobby or a skill to share, and be able to travel independently. The fund carefully matches visitors’ profiles with clients - for example, a visually impaired person who is a talented musician is matched with an elderly person who enjoys…
innovations.benef: Czech Radio Endowment Fund, Together with You
innovations.evidence: In total, 27 people have been employed as visitors since the beginning of the project. Currently, the start-up employs 10 visitors, who operate in seven cities across Czechia. Since the beginning of the project, visually impaired people have visited over 600 elderly people and have spent more than 4 200 hours with them. The employees have monthly meetings where they can share their experience with others, which has proved to be an effective team-building activity. Over the years, visually impaired people have gained more responsibility in running the sessions, managing their regular work…
authors: Czech Radio Endowment Fund, Together with You

innovations.name: Empleando Digital
innovations.problem: The demand for digital skills in the workplace is growing rapidly, and it is estimated that 9 out of 10 jobs will require digital skills in the near future . This means that some level of knowledge of advanced digital skills - such as coding or debugging - will be increasingly required for entry into many jobs, barring access to people with low qualifications . For people from vulnerable backgrounds, such as the Roma community, this could mean an increased risk of exclusion from the labour market and further economic hardship if they do not have access to digital and technological training. The Spanish work force lags behind the EU average in terms of digital skills, and this shortcoming is…
innovations.desc: EmpleandoDigital (Employing Digital) offers a tailored digital skills training programme for people at risk of social exclusion. The Fundación Secretariado Gitano (FSG) was established in the 1960’s to protect the rights of the Roma community in Spain, improve their living conditions and prevent all kinds of discrimination against this community. The social action NGO achieves this  through a series of programmes including Acceder , which focuses on promoting labour market inclusion among the Roma community through tailored Individual Employment Plans (IEPs) and the establishment of strategic alliances with potential employers. #EmpleandoDigital , launched at the end of 2017, brings the Acceder programme into the digital era, focusing on developing the digital skills of people at risk of social exclusion through a digital skills training scheme. While similar projects exist in Spain,…
innovations.benef: Fundacion Secretariado Gitano, Spanish Red Cross, Accenture Foundation
innovations.evidence: From 2017–2019, #EmpleandoDigital was deployed in 12 out of 17 Spanish regions, with over 300 professionals from 26 employment teams in FSG and the Red Cross directly involved in the project. A total of 9 826 people at risk of exclusion participated in the project, improving their digital skills and knowledge. Of these, 5 924 people improved their digital skills through basic courses, and 2 328 have taken an advanced course. A total of 235 people attended one of the 23 courses in occupations that are being modified by digital transformation. Furthermore, 48 people participated in the 4…
authors: Fundacion Secretariado Gitano, Spanish Red Cross, Accenture Foundation

innovations.name: Portugal Social Innovation
innovations.problem: Portugal Social Innovation initiative was created in December 2014, within a very specific national context that aligned the needs, the players and the funding. After Ireland and Greece, in May 2011, at the peak of the European sovereign debt crisis, Portugal signed a three-year Economic Adjustment Programme with the EU, the European Central Bank (ECB) and the International Monetary Fund (IMF). Strong austerity measures followed, increasing social needs. Those increasing social needs were being met by a combination of diverse deep-rooted traditional social economy players (associations, foundations, cooperatives, church-based organisations, etc.), as well as by an emerging group of social…
innovations.desc:
Portugal Social Innovation (PSI) is a pioneering public policy initiative that aims to promote social innovation and entrepreneurship, and develop the social investment market in Portugal. It does so by encouraging collaboration between investors and social entrepreneurs to promote social innovation projects. The goal of this initiative is to support the development and scaling of new solutions addressing social problems which complement more traditional and conventional ones. To do so, four instruments were created to address the specific financing needs of innovative social organisations and social entrepreneurs, also assuming the active involvement of public and private investors in the process as partners that can contribute to the economic and financial sustainability of the projects.
According to The Economist’s Social Innovation Index 2016 , Portugal is one of only seven…
innovations.evidence:
Portugal is currently heralded as the pioneer of national policies on social innovation.
Up to this date, there were 18 open Calls for Proposals that received in total 1.244 applications, of which 693 were approved. This represents a total of EUR 148 million used, of which EUR 99 million are ESF funding and EUR 49 million are social investment mobilised in the market.
Currently PSI deals directly with 477 entrepreneurial organizations and 841 social investors, including corporations, municipalities, foundations, banks, funds among others, financing projects with potential for impacting around…

innovations.name: V/Faktor
innovations.problem: In Austria, levels of rural unemployment and financial deprivation are among the lowest in the European Union . However, there are particularly high levels of high-skilled emigration from rural to urban areas among women and young parents, which has raised concerns about the future prosperity of Austria’s rural areas. Excessive rural emigration among skilled workers can lead to long-term economic stagnation in affected areas. Retaining skilled workers in areas with high emigration is therefore a critical way of preventing and minimising regional wealth inequality.
innovations.desc:
V/Faktor (2017–2019) was a pilot project launched in three rural regions of Austria with high levels of emigration of skilled workers. It aimed to reduce emigration by making employment in rural areas more appealing than moving to cities.
Project partners worked closely with regional teams and local businesses, offering a tailored consultation process to design and implement work-life and family-life balance measures in the region that actually worked. Measures to improve the work-life balance of employees are traditionally organised through national legislation or at the initiative of individual companies. V/Faktor, on the other hand, worked at the regional level by fostering partnerships between businesses, municipal authorities, and other stakeholders to develop innovative and locally relevant work-life balance initiatives.
The project conducted an initial consultation to understand…
innovations.benef: ABZ*AUSTRIA, ÖAR GmbH, BAB Unternehmensberatung GmbH
innovations.evidence: Some examples of successful initiatives following participation in the project include development of internal company childcare facilities, introduction of remote working opportunities, improvement of parental leave management, strengthening of female entrepreneurs, improved reconciliation for female leaders, corporate gender equality plans and management training modules.
authors: ABZ*AUSTRIA, ÖAR GmbH, BAB Unternehmensberatung GmbH

innovations.name: Curing the Limbo
innovations.problem: By 2020, there were more than 100 000 refugees living in Greece, with 15 000-20 000 estimated to be living in the capital, Athens. Many of these individuals have been economically inactive for extended periods of time, while staying in temporary accommodation. A decade after the economic and financial crisis, the city is still facing high unemployment rates, which in turn makes it even more difficult for refugees to enter the labour market.
innovations.desc:
Curing the Limbo aims to actively support refugees to exit the state of ‘limbo’ caused by long-term inactivity and an overall feeling of uncertainty. It is an inclusive integration initiative to help refugees and vulnerable groups create strong bonds with their local communities, acquire new skills, solve local problems together with active citizens, and build self-confidence. These are all qualities that are essential for their development as responsible citizens.
The programme is innovative in its holistic approach, which actively involves local residents. City activities that refugees can take part in are identified by project partners and co-designed with local community groups based on a co-creation methodology developed by synAthina , the civil society platform of the city of Athens. This bridges the gap between locals and new residents in a creative way, allowing the community to…
innovations.benef: Municipality of Athens, International Rescue Committee Hellas, Catholic Relief Services
innovations.evidence: Through the civil society platform of the Athens Municipality, synAthina, 200 refugees are taking part in 488 community activities with active local citizens, and are being empowered to collaborate and co-design activities that have a positive impact in their neighbourhoods. The programme is ongoing and results are not yet fully available. At the end of the three-year period, programme participants will have developed language skills, received support with transitioning to longer-term housing solutions, and been given access to a network of active and engaged local people, as well as to…

innovations.name: GVETS: Introducing Gamification in Vocational Education and Training
innovations.problem: According to the IOM and UNICEF (2016), one in five refugees and migrants who have crossed the Mediterranean Sea to Europe is a child. They estimate that 214 355 migrant children from third countries arrived in EU Member States in 2016 alone . This increase in the number of migrant children arriving in Europe has challenged organisations’ capacity to respond to their particular psychological and social needs, particularly given limited resources and expertise.
innovations.desc:
Gamification in Vocational Education and Training for Professionals and Social Workers (GVETS) is an interdisciplinary capacity-building programme for professionals working with migrant children. GVETS was set up as an Erasmus+ project, by a Consortium led by the Centre for Social Innovation (CSI) in Cyprus. The Consortium includes partners from Portugal, Hungary, Lithuania, Greece, Italy and Spain.
The programme uses the innovative pedagogical method of gamification to increase the skills of social workers when working with migrant children, through an online learning platform. The programme consists of seven chapters/topics – protection of migrant children, working with migrant children at risk, crisis management, civic education and professional guidance for minors with a migratory background, critical and constructive practice in social work, social workers working with migrant…
innovations.benef: Menedék-Hungarian Association for Migrants, Center for Social Innovation - CSI, IASIS NGO, ITAINNOVA, Oxfam Italia, AIDGLOBAL - Acção e Integração para o Desenvolvimento Global, Diversity Development Group
innovations.evidence:
The course has been developed in alignment with university courses, allowing its integration, certification and accreditation to be validated through different European frameworks, such as the European Qualifications Framework (EQF), the European Credit system for Vocational Education and Training (ECVET) and European Quality Assurance in Vocational Education and Training (EQAVET).
The online training course prototype was launched for testing among the community of experts and completed at the end of 2019. Engagement so far shows that there has been a positive impact on increasing the…
authors: Menedék-Hungarian Association for Migrants, Center for Social Innovation - CSI, IASIS NGO, ITAINNOVA, Oxfam Italia, AIDGLOBAL - Acção e Integração para o Desenvolvimento Global, Diversity Development Group

innovations.name: Regseda
innovations.problem: People with disabilities often feel isolated and excluded from society, with working opportunities often scarce and unsustainable.  Since the country’s independence in 1990, the Lithuanian government has made significant efforts to improve employment opportunities and social inclusion for people with disabilities. However, these issues are still present in Lithuania. Data from 2018 shows that approximately 8% of the Lithuanian population are classified as disabled, and most are outside the labour market. The proportion of people with a disability at risk of poverty or social exclusion in Lithuania is at 43%, the third highest rate in the EU (compared to an EU average of 28.7%).
innovations.desc:
Regseda is a social enterprise in Lithuania that has recognised the long-term problem of social inclusion and employment of people with disabilities in the country, and has been employing people with various disabilities, and specifically visual impairments, since 1959. Regseda began as a factory producing cardboard and packaging materials in Klaipėda, Lithuania, employing mainly blind workers. Since then, it has become one of the largest social enterprises in the country. Regseda employs and trains people with visual, auditory, nervous system, behavioural and movement disorders to assemble and manufacture products for the factory. Workers are encouraged to help each other to increase efficiency. Hearing impaired people might verify the work carried out by visually impaired people, for example,.
The innovation of Regseda is that it empowers this vulnerable group beyond training alone.…
innovations.target: Long-term or repeatedly unemployed persons, Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised
innovations.evidence:
Between 2009 and 2018, Regseda tripled its number of employees, and today it employs 196 people. 155 of these are people with disabilities, 84 of which have a visual impairment. Regseda creates 2-3 new jobs every year. The company is now the supplier of goods for the largest furniture producers in the country and internationally, supplying companies such as IKEA, as well as smaller producers from Lithuania, Sweden, and Germany.
In financial terms, in 2016, the company generated a turnover of EUR 3.2 million. The growth of the company has enabled the purchase of new equipment and machinery,…

innovations.name: Wings of Hope
innovations.problem: In 2016, 1 429 children lived in childcare institutions in Latvia. Whilst these institutions were originally created to provide vulnerable groups with care and shelter, evidence has shown that they are not effective in supporting people to participate fully in their community and wider society. The process of ‘deinstitutionalisation’ has been high on the political agenda of the European Union, supported by the UN Conventions on the Rights of the Child and on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities . Latvia’s 2015 social service reform and deinstitutionalisation policy, supported by the European Social Fund, has seen local municipalities, long-term care institutions and non-governmental…
innovations.desc:
Founded in Latvia in 2003, Cerību Spārni , or Wings of Hope, improves community life for children and young people with various disabilities. The association operates in the town of Sigulda. Wings of Hope is innovative in that it focuses on empowering beneficiaries to fully integrate into the activities of daily life. It is also the only association in Latvia that offers its services to all age groups, as most other similar projects focus only on young children.
Children and young people with disabilities participate in activities that help to familiarise them with household tasks, to build their independence and self-sufficiency. They take part in workshops that use new and innovative educational methods, including dance and movement therapy, art and music therapy, sand therapy and speech therapy . The association also provides theatre classes, logistics classes and therapeutic…
innovations.benef: Wings of Hope, Sigulda Municipality, State Employment Agency
innovations.evidence: In 2016, Wings of Hope provided services to 54 families in need, and went beyond the boundaries of Sigulda, reaching people in four nearby towns. Four young people with disabilities were successfully integrated into the open labour market after working for Wings of Hope. The charity shop is projected to be able to provide paid employment to people with disabilities over the next 10 years. The social services provided by the Wings of Hope association have particularly benefited the parents and family members of children with disabilities, 97% of whom are now working in the regular labour…
authors: Wings of Hope, Sigulda Municipality, State Employment Agency

innovations.name: IMPROVE
innovations.problem: The demographic structure of Sweden has changed in recent decades, with young people increasingly migrating from rural areas and an ageing population. 12.5% of the total population in Sweden lives in rural areas (1.28 million people), while 20% of the total population (more than 2 million people) is above 65. This comes with challenges for public services, which are often unable to reach people in rural and remote places due to shortages of skilled staff, high costs of services and less developed transportation services. Rural municipalities of Sweden have also seen a change in community engagement, with older people participating increasingly less in social activities.
innovations.desc:
IMPROVE (‘Involving the community to co-produce public services’) aims to give those in rural and remote areas equal access to the latest service solutions, through technology. IMPROVE helps people to design and deliver their own public services. The project is based on ‘living labs’, workshops where local citizens meet with service providers and public authorities, with the aim of finding solutions to common community problems. This co-production shifts the balance of power, responsibility and resources from professionals to the individuals that use public services. In the ‘living labs’, providers, users and public authorities are equally responsible for designing the services. This process makes them more accessible, more relevant to people’s needs, more targeted and more cost-effective.
The project was implemented in the six areas of the EU Northern Periphery and Arctic programme…
innovations.benef: Association of Local Authorities, Västernorrland County, ERNACT, European Regions Network for the Application of Communications Technology, Municipality of Kramfors (Swedish: Kramfors kommun)
innovations.evidence: The IMPROVE project has had a profound positive impact on the communities of Västernorrland by making public services more accessible and more efficient. It has given people in remote and rural areas access to innovative life-improving technologies that they would not otherwise have had. The public services co-created and delivered in the seven municipalities of Västernorrland focused mostly on healthcare and wellbeing, using technologies such as e-health or smart homes for elderly people. Four main products were developed. The first, a key-free lock, uses an app to unlock the front doors of…
authors: Association of Local Authorities, Västernorrland County, ERNACT, European Regions Network for the Application of Communications Technology, Municipality of Kramfors (Swedish: Kramfors kommun)

innovations.name: Local Agenda 21 Plus Vienna
innovations.problem: In an increasingly connected world, the lack of communication and cooperation between local governments and citizens is a growing concern. It can lead to mistrust among citizens of governing institutions and general societal unrest. This can, in turn, hinder the implementation of measures that require behavioural change in citizens, as they are less trustful of public authority and less engaged in local life. Community-led solutions are an important way of building trust between citizens and government and ensuring that solutions to problems are sustainable and long-lasting.
innovations.desc:
Local Agenda 21 was launched at the United Nations Conference on Environment and Development in 1992, known as the Rio Summit. It is a governance model that aims to promote grassroots democracy, sustainable development and improved communication between citizens and public authorities at the district level. In Vienna, Austria, it led to the implementation of the Local Agenda 21 from 2002 to 2009, renamed Local Agenda 21 Plus (LA21+) from 2009 to 2014.
LA21+ is implemented by the LA21+ Association. ‘Agenda Offices’ have been set up in participating districts in the city to motivate citizens to take part in shaping the sustainable development of their district. Citizens of all backgrounds meet to discuss and identify local needs and ideas for development. The Agenda Office can help implement these ideas. Ideas vary depending on the requests of the citizens and the district, but their core…
innovations.benef: Local Agenda 21 Plus Vienna, MA18 Municipal Department of Urban Development
innovations.evidence: Between September 2009 and 2014, six districts of Vienna implemented LA21+. Due to the wide range of activities that LA21+ covers, there have been a wide variety of results. Within the area of Donaustadt, for example, citizens’ ideas that were implemented included improving cycling infrastructure with more bicycle parking spaces and interconnecting cycle lanes, and the development of a new community garden, with increased networking between cultures. In Josefstadt, a public neighbourhood ‘meeting zone’ was created, city gardens were built to reduce the urban heat island effect, and a ‘buy…
authors: Local Agenda 21 Plus Vienna, MA18 Municipal Department of Urban Development

innovations.name: Garden of Encounter
innovations.problem: In 2015, Europe experienced a flow of refugees crossing into its borders to escape the conflict in Syria. Many European countries are still struggling to deal with this crisis. In Austria, the largest refugee camp grew around the village of Traiskirchen. In 2015, 1 500 people were found to be sleeping in the open air in ‘inhumane’ conditions at the camp . Refugees were left waiting in the camp during their legal proceedings, with little to no activities, and with no connection to the local community in Austria.
innovations.desc: The Garden of Encounter (GoE) began in 2016 following demands from community members and refugees for a space to connect with one another. The municipal authority of Traiskirchen provided the GoE project with EUR 36 000, a 10 000m2 plot of land with 200 fruit trees, and gave it access to the local youth centre building. The Garden brings people together regardless of nationality, religion and age, offering refugees low threshold integration activities and the local community a chance to engage with its new residents. The communal space encourages connection and collaboration between community members and refugees. The garden is open three days a week. It also acts as an educational space, hosting sewing workshops, German language classes, legal advice and emotional support groups for refugees. It hosts three school class visits per week for schools and local scout groups, in order to…
innovations.benef: Garden of Encounter, Respekt.net, Snapshots from the Border
innovations.evidence:
In the three years since the project’s initiation, GoE has involved approximately 100 refugees in its activities, with 30 currently volunteering at the community garden and sewing workshop. The GoE team wrote recommendation letters for, and accompanied many of the refugees to, asylum hearings, resulting in 50% of them being granted asylum.
The GoE team reported that the psycho-emotional impact of the initiative on refugees has been impressive, as the garden and workshops have given them stability, a distraction and something to care for during this uncertain period of their life. One…
authors: Garden of Encounter, Respekt.net, Snapshots from the Border

innovations.name: Village Hub
innovations.problem: Across Europe, a large share of people with disabilities still face barriers to integrating into the labour market. Due to difficulties in finding work adapted to their needs and/or capacities, people with disabilities are, on average, twice as likely to remain inactive or long-term unemployed than other groups. In the case of those living in remote or rural areas such as Beveren-aan-de-IJzer, in the Westhoek region of Flanders, Belgium, they can face further risk of social exclusion due to fewer available opportunities for training and work. Moreover, remote areas amplify the difficulties for disabled people in accessing public services, transportation or cultural and leisure opportunities…
innovations.desc: The Village Hub (Dorpspunt) in Beveren was launched in 2017, with the aim of increasing social inclusion and restoring services to the remote region. The Village Hub is a multi-purpose store, delivering a range of in-demand services. These include the sale of locally-sourced agricultural products, such as fruit and vegetables, dairy and meat products, bread and pastries; the provision of a meeting place where people can drink coffee and chat; and the provision of a mobility hub that offers people the opportunity to carpool, borrow a bike, rent an e-bike or have their bike repaired. While similar projects exist in larger cities, the Village Hub is unique in its scale and location within the remote village of Beveren, an area that suffers from poor public transportation, few job opportunities and a lack of spaces for communal living and exchange. It is also unique in that it is people…

(formerly known as Dorpsdienst Nestor)
innovations.evidence: Since its creation three years ago, the Village Hub has involved approximately 30 volunteers, around nine of whom are involved in the store on a daily basis. The hub provides practical work experience and a social outlet for people with disabilities. It has also benefited the local community with its services, as these were in high-demand and not provided before. The social aspect has been the most important result, as the social meeting point created has been more successful than predicted, reaching more than 50% of the villagers within the local area. Community members provide regular…

De Lovie vzw, Taxistop, Town council of Alveringem, Yellow Window, Nestor+

innovations.name: CAP Markets
innovations.problem: In 2017, the employment rate of people without a disability was 82%, while for people with a disability it was 55%, and for people with a severe disability it was 48% . Employers may be cautious about employing people with a disability due to worries over capability and skills. Usually, sheltered workshops and social enterprises that hire people with disabilities offer them jobs that do not involve direct contact with the public. This may limit their interaction with the local community and possibly hamper their full social inclusion in daily life.
innovations.desc:
CAP Market, taking its name from ‘handicap’, is a food market store that provides employment opportunities for people with disabilities. The first CAP Market opened in Germany in 1999, with the aim of creating a space for people with disabilities to work together, as well as with people without a disability. CAP Markets offer 50% of their jobs – of both back office and people-facing roles – to people with disabilities, providing them with a near-normal working life and the chance to fully integrate into the local community.
CAP Market is run by gdw süd , a social cooperative that organises workshops for people who have disabilities. They use their expertise in partnering with services and social enterprises that offer employment to the same demographic. Typically, local authorities approach gdw süd with a proposal to re-occupy empty shops. gdw süd then seeks a franchise partner to open…
innovations.target: Individuals with disabilities, Other target groups
innovations.evidence:
Having grown in popularity since their creation in 1999, there are now 107 CAP Markets running throughout Germany in almost all federal states, each serving a geographical area of approximately 4 000 inhabitants. CAP Markets currently have 1 555 employees, of which around 850 have a disability. This creates an inclusive working environment and a more cohesive community through constant contact and communication between workers and customers.
The markets have also reintroduced valuable services to the communities. By locating shops and services in disused existing market locations, they have…

innovations.name: Dialogmuseum Frankfurt
innovations.problem: People who are blind and partially sighted are the disability group with the lowest employment rate in Europe. The biggest obstacle for visually impaired job seekers is not their disability itself, but rather prejudice. There is a lack of general knowledge about what blind people can and cannot do, with a resultant prejudice against hiring or working with them . These prejudices can be overcome through interaction, as people learn from encounters and experiences. However, spaces where people with and without disabilities can interact and respectfully learn from each other are rare.
innovations.desc:
Dialogmuseum (DM) Frankfurt aims to provide such spaces for interaction and learning, while also providing employment for people with disabilities. The ambassadors and tour guides at DM are people who have a visual impairment. DM offers visitors the opportunity to experience parts of the world in complete darkness. It gives them an insight into the life of a visually impaired person, while being guided around the exhibit by one. The intention is to create a role reversal, where the visually impaired person is the expert and the visitors must trust in their guide. The guided tour lasts 60 minutes, visiting four adventure rooms, or 90 minutes, visiting six adventure rooms. Each guided group consists of eight people and one visually impaired guide.
Dialogmuseum (DM) in Frankurt was founded in 2005 as a follow-up to the ‘ Dialogue in the Dark ’ project, which seeks to create exhibition…
innovations.evidence:
By the end of 2016, DM had 26 full-time employees, nine temporary staff and three volunteers.
Approximately 70% of all visitors to the museum are young people in education. DM works with schools, providing teachers with educational materials to prepare for and follow-up on the experience. After finding that only 10% of teachers who visit the museum use them, these materials have been made more widely accessible and available for free download on DM’s website, entitled ‘The Pedagogical Booklet’. In addition, DM has developed the ‘Invisible Friend’ project, offering children the chance to tour…

innovations.name: NEO
innovations.problem: One in three women have experienced some form of physical and/or sexual violence since the age of 15, according to the most recent Fundamental Rights Agency report on violence against women in Europe . Gender-based violence harms women, families, communities and societies. It is a human rights violation, and one of the most pervasive forms of gender-based inequality. In Spain, there has been an increasing focus on gender issues, with six national plans for equality being implemented over the past 20 years, including the 2004 Comprehensive Law Against Gender Violence and the 2007 Equality Law. While Spain has made notable improvements in this field , there is much that remains to be done,…
innovations.desc:
The NEO project, founded in 2018 by the Cepaim Foundation , aims to understand men’s life experiences in order to shape them into allies in the fight for gender equality. Whereas previous approaches to improving gender equality have focused on legal equality between men and women, the NEO project’s  innovative approach is in trying to tackle the issues of gender inequality by focusing on masculinity, and the role it plays in gender equality.
Through participatory workshops and awareness events, the NEO project builds on the Cepaim Foundation’s previous work in developing innovative group methodologies to work with men by expanding the project to other workplaces in public and private institutions, and analysing current gender roles in the workplace, existing barriers to change, how work is organised among workers and differences in opportunity between men and women. The project also…
innovations.evidence: By addressing gender inequality from the perspective of men, and involving them is discussions on how to address it, the NEO project has targeted people that are not usually included in initiatives on the topic. NEO has moved gender issues away from being a ‘women only’ concern, by increasing ownership and awareness of the impact of gender equality solutions among men as well. Through NEO and Campaign 365, the Cepaim Foundation has held various awareness-raising events and focused on the key role that men can play in gender equality issues. It has also hosted ‘Men, Employment and Care’…

innovations.name: My Streets Ireland
innovations.problem: There is often a stigma surrounding homelessness in Ireland. People can be denied opportunities and be socially excluded if they have experienced, or are experiencing, homelessness. The economic crisis in 2008 and the lack of sufficient social housing saw the beginnings of a rise in homelessness in the country. In January 2020, there were over 10 000 homeless adults and children in Ireland . The town of Drogheda has only two emergency accommodation facilities for homeless people, which cannot meet the increasing demand. At the same time, there has been a lack of uptake of educational courses offered to homeless people , and there are limited education opportunities suited to individuals…
innovations.desc:
My Streets Ireland (MSI) was formed with the aim of increasing educational and employment opportunities for homeless people. Founded in 2014, the social enterprise My Streets Ireland teaches homeless people the art of storytelling through tailored education programmes, and provides them with the opportunity to progress to become a paid walking tour guide. Anyone who is, or was, homeless can access the programme through a referral system from the local homeless services, with the only requirement that the person is sober, and hence demonstrates psychological stability, before graduating and becoming a paid walking tour guide. Tours can then be booked by anyone, through the MSI website.
The City of Dublin Education and Training Board (CDETB), the Dublin-based charity Fighting Words, professional storytellers at Candlelit Tales, and the local historian Reamonn Mac Aodhagáin deliver a…
innovations.benef: My Streets Ireland, Fighting Words, Candlelit Tales, Community of Dublin Education and training Board
innovations.evidence: Since 2014, 51 people have been trained by MSI. Over 50% of the trainees, some of whom have literacy issues, have progressed onto further education or employment, or have found accommodation within six months of completing the programme. Currently, there are a further 15 new recruits undergoing the MSI three-month training programme. It should be noted that more people have engaged with the training programme and not necessarily progressed onto a position as a tour guide, as it is not a requirement. Those that did progress have served approximately 11 000 customers to date, earning an average…
authors: My Streets Ireland, Fighting Words, Candlelit Tales, Community of Dublin Education and training Board

innovations.name: Social Innovation under the European Social Fund in Flanders
innovations.problem: Social innovators may encounter certain obstacles when designing and implementing projects directly funded by the national or regional programmes of European Social Fund (ESF). Having to deliver on ambitious outputs – such as a high number of beneficiaries or inclusive employment outcomes – may hinder the engagement of smaller organisations in experimental projects, particularly those that do not have access to expert guidance and support. A 2018 study on beneficiaries’ experiences of the ESF by the European Parliament showed that around 90% of beneficiaries think that more support is required to enable them to fully participate in the ESF, particularly for NGOs and small private operators.
innovations.desc:
The region of Flanders in Belgium, which has allocated 8.5% of its overall ESF budget (EUR 33.8 million) to social innovation priorities, has addressed this challenge by introducing and developing a dedicated support package of guidance, tools and capacity-building services for socially innovative organisations using the ESF. The support aims to help social innovation projects in their design, implementation and scale-up.
To receive funding, proposals need to have an explicit focus on the interaction between service providers and users, where the user is the employed person or jobseeker facing a specific social or labour challenge. Hence, the focus is on providing innovative services that directly benefit users. The calls for funding are published on a regular basis and structured into two different types:
innovation via exploration – for projects that want to start with a societal…
innovations.target: Other target groups
innovations.benef: ESF Flanders, Antwerp Management School (Flanders Inshape), Social Innovation Factory, Flanders District of Creativity
innovations.evidence: By 2018, there were 4 rounds of calls and 93 projects had applied for funding – 35 for innovation via exploration and 58 for innovation via adaptation. The projects covered the following topics: adapting to change, active inclusion, entrepreneurship, lifelong learning and reducing early school leaving. A large proportion of the projects submitted and selected had a specific focus on vulnerable groups such as migrants, people with disabilities and people and families in poverty. Others focused on human resources, reducing early school leaving, lifelong learning and developing future-oriented…
authors: ESF Flanders, Antwerp Management School (Flanders Inshape), Social Innovation Factory, Flanders District of Creativity

innovations.name: Community-Led Local Development in Kujawsko-Pomorskie
innovations.problem: Kujawsko-Pomorskie, a province in northern Poland, has the highest level of unemployment in the country (4% compared to a 2.9% national average ) and the third-highest share of the population living below the national poverty line (17.5%). It is a region with many vulnerable groups, particularly women, that are unemployed on a long-term basis and an ageing community with an increasing number of people on social benefits. Solutions to support these groups have often been developed in a top-down way, without the involvement of target groups themselves or local actors. This approach fails to take into consideration their needs and to promote ownership and sustainability of the solutions.
innovations.desc:
In 2016, the European Social Fund (ESF) Managing Authority of Kujawsko-Pomorskie developed a community-led local development (CLLD) strategy to empower local actors in various parts of the region to use the regional programmes of all European structural and investment funds to tackle social issues in a bottom-up way. The CLLD strategy aims to develop local infrastructure and facilitate the integration into employment and social inclusion of the most deprived in the region. It directly supports local initiatives in both cities and rural areas of the region with a total of EUR 36.5 million, made available through the European Regional Development Fund (ERDF), the ESF, European Agricultural Fund for Rural Development (EAFRD) and the European Maritime and Fisheries Fund (EMFF)
To implement the strategy, 28 local action groups (LAGs) have been set up in Kujawsko-Pomorskie. The LAGs are made…
innovations.benef: ESF Managing Authority - Region of Kujawsko-Pomorskie, Local Action Group of Bydgoszcz Assiociation "Two Rivers", The Partnership for Krajna and Pałuki Association (Local Action Group)
innovations.evidence: Overall, almost 100 calls for proposals have been issued by 26 different LAGs and approximately 500 applications have been received. Since 2016, 327 projects have been funded through the CLLD strategy. For example, the People with Disabilities – Conscious Participant Movement project targeted people of all ages and with all types of disabilities. The project offered participants the opportunity to get involved in physical exercise sessions, to receive psychological support and to attend workshops and educational lectures on several topics (theatre lessons, driving classes, etc.). A similar…
authors: ESF Managing Authority - Region of Kujawsko-Pomorskie, Local Action Group of Bydgoszcz Assiociation "Two Rivers", The Partnership for Krajna and Pałuki Association (Local Action Group)

innovations.name: Entrepreneurially, into the world of business HRT
innovations.problem: In Slovenia, approximately 10% of young people with upper-secondary and post-secondary education are unemployed. At the same time, the rate of self-employment in Slovenia (13%) remains below the EU average (14%). The Zasavje area, once a highly developed coal-mining and industrial region, is facing a rapid loss of jobs and limited investment in new business ventures, leaving young people with limited opportunities.
innovations.desc:
The Entrepreneurially, into the world of business HRT scheme provides participants that are registered as unemployed, regardless of their gender, age or education and with permanent residence within the Zasavje region, with financial support, full-time training opportunities and guidance from internal and external mentors, coaches and recognised entrepreneurs to develop their own business ideas. The scheme is based on its predecessor of the same name, which was implemented by the Slovenian Ministry of Economic Development and Technology in cooperation with 12 regional development agencies (RDAs) in the country. The scheme stands apart from similar youth entrepreneurship programmes due to the role of the RDAs.
Young people respond to a public call to submit an idea aimed at fostering social innovation in areas such as employment, digitalisation or mobility. The scheme strongly encourages…
innovations.benef: Zasavje Regional Development Agency, Development Centre Novo mesto, Regional Development Agency for Gorenjska, BSC Kranj, Regional Development Agency for Koroška (RRA Koroška), Regional development Agency Posavje, Regional development agency Zeleni Kras
innovations.evidence: The project proved to be highly successful in its pilot phase within the Zasavje region. It has subsequently been implemented at the national level. It has grown from a project supporting 40 participants at pilot level, to one with 360 participants and a 60% success rate ( 2014 national project ). The monitoring data collected by the project representatives show that, in 2017–2018, 16 new enterprises or start-ups were established thanks to the project. By 2019, approximately 75% of beneficiaries had either started their own business or found employment. In the Zasavje region, different…
authors: Zasavje Regional Development Agency, Development Centre Novo mesto, Regional Development Agency for Gorenjska, BSC Kranj, Regional Development Agency for Koroška (RRA Koroška), Regional development Agency Posavje, Regional development agency Zeleni Kras

innovations.name: JUVENTUS
innovations.problem: The EU has a long tradition of transnational mobility programmes, such as Leonardo and Erasmus+ , supporting youth studying and working abroad. This benefits students and trainees by helping them define their career choices and secure their first job. However, less than one quarter of beneficiaries of these programmes are young people from socially and economically disadvantaged backgrounds, such as young people not in education, employment or training (NEETs). By 2019, it was estimated that there were approximately 9.3 million NEETs across the EU. According to the Erasmus+ evaluation , young people from disadvantaged backgrounds, in particular those who are disengaged or at risk of…
innovations.desc: JUVENTUS is an approach to innovative exchange programmes targeting young people from disadvantaged backgrounds, particularly NEETs, with the aim of enhancing their employability through internships abroad. The approach was introduced in 2016 by the European Social Fund’s (ESF’s) Learning Network on Transnational Mobility Measures for Disadvantaged Youth and Young Adults (TLN Mobility). The network was created in 2013. It formed a new partnership between ESF managing and implementing authorities from 15 different EU Member States and regions to support the planning of transnational mobility measures targeting vulnerable groups through national and regional ESF 2014–2020 programmes. TLN Mobility developed a coordinated call, including a manual of guidance, that acts as a common framework to facilitate transnational synchronisation and harmonisation of national schemes. The manual…
innovations.target: NEETs (Not in Education, Employment, or Training)
innovations.benef: Bundesministerium für Arbeit und Soziales (BMAS), ESF Unit, Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs (Czechia), Servizio Europa- Ufficio Fondo Sociale Europeo- Agenzia del Lavoro, Ministerstwo Funduszy i Polityki Regionalnej, Department for ESF Management, Servicio Andaluz de Empleo (SAE), Employment Service of Slovenia, Svenska ESF-rådet
innovations.evidence: The JUVENTUS approach provides NEETs aged 18–35 with a practical opportunity to find their way in a foreign country. Due to its architecture of transnational harmonisation and synchronisation of operational, funding and matchmaking arrangements, JUVENTUS has successfully included a diverse range of NEETs in its transnational exchange programmes including long-term unemployed, people early school leavers, or those with a migration background. This is largely attributed to the non-financial support measures offered to participants before and after their exchange, which also leads to high…
authors: Bundesministerium für Arbeit und Soziales (BMAS), ESF Unit, Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs (Czechia), Servizio Europa- Ufficio Fondo Sociale Europeo- Agenzia del Lavoro, Ministerstwo Funduszy i Polityki Regionalnej, Department for ESF Management, Servicio Andaluz de Empleo (SAE), Employment Service of Slovenia, Svenska ESF-rådet

innovations.name: Emerging Young Entrepreneurs (EYES)
innovations.problem: In both Slovakia and Hungary, young people under the age of 25 are around three times more likely to be unemployed (11.4% in Hungary and 16.1% in Slovakia) than the rest of the adult population (3.4% in Hungary and 5.8% in Slovakia). This is due to a mix of structural barriers (e.g. skill mismatches) and cyclical factors (economic upturns and downturns). Stimulating youth entrepreneurship is one approach to addressing this challenge. However, entrepreneurship education is not widely taught at schools. Opportunities to experiment with entrepreneurial ideas and meet and learn from entrepreneurs are rare in formal education in Slovakia and Hungary. This gives young people little chance to…
innovations.desc:
The Emerging Young Entrepreneurs (EYES) programme provided training and business opportunities to young entrepreneurs under the age of 25 from both Slovakia and Hungary. The programme, which ran from September 2017 to April 2019, was the only programme in the region to focus specifically on upskilling young potential entrepreneurs through educational events, training and networking opportunities across two countries. The programme also aimed to increase labour mobility and cooperation between public institutions, communities and companies on either side of the border.
The programme ran start-up competitions to propel promising new entrepreneurs into the business space, as well as networking events for emerging entrepreneurs and national and cross-border events for sharing experiences. The programme combined theoretical learning with hands-on support. One of the activities, for example,…
innovations.benef: Budapest Enterprise Agency (BEA), Slovak University of Technology, Hungarian National Trading House
innovations.evidence:
The EYES programme provided educational and networking opportunities to over 300 start-ups in the region and delivered many key learning events. Over 18 months, it reached a vast audience of 10 000 people – 10 times more people than planned – in the form of views, likes, shares and comments on its social media activities and online articles.
The events run by the programme were deemed successful. The Budapest Start-up Night, in November 2018, was attended by more than 600 people. The event was accompanied by business-to-business networking, an exhibition and an award ceremony, and had…
authors: Budapest Enterprise Agency (BEA), Slovak University of Technology, Hungarian National Trading House

innovations.name: Prepare Me
innovations.problem: Activities such as going shopping, eating in a restaurant, using public transportation or visiting a doctor are seen as ‘normal’ everyday activities by many. However, they can be a cause of stress and anxiety for individuals with additional needs due to an intellectual disability or autism. Carrying out such activities may cause distress to these individuals as they are unsure of what to expect or what is expected of them. Thus, they may refuse to participate in these activities altogether, putting them at an increased risk of social isolation and exclusion. Families and carers face challenges in understanding how they can effectively prepare adults or children with additional needs to gain…
